articles.title_orig: Stocks, Nasdaq Futures Climb as AI Trade Rebounds: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Stocks, Nasdaq Futures Climb as AI Trade Rebounds: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Global stocks rallied on Thursday, staging a tentative recovery from an intense AI-driven sell-off and looked past a fresh set of tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and will have a shortened trading session on Friday. During Wednesday's regular session, the Dow gained 0.33%, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62% and the S&P 500 shed 0.25%, with the major averages paring losses seen earlier in the trading day.
In Europe on Thursday, equities rose sharply. The pan-European Stoxx 600 was 1.6% higher by 12:20 p.m. in London (7:20 a.m. ET), with all sectors and major bourses in positive territory.
Germany's DAX led gains on a rise of 1.9%, while the Stoxx 600 Technology index jumped 2.5%. The regional tech index has lost around 12% so far this month, amid jitters around a potential AI bubble bursting and the ousting — and return — of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO.
German semiconductor firm Infineon was more than 4% higher in afternoon trading, as chip stocks notched a boost. ASMI and ASML each gained just over 3%, while Be Semiconductor added 3.5%.
Asia-Pacific markets also rose on Thursday, with regional tech stocks also rebounded sharply, led by Japanese chip-related companies.
South Korea's Kospi gained 0.29% to close at 4,711.21, while the small-cap Kosdaq index advanced 0.78% to 655.71 after the country's central bank hiked benchmark lending rates to a 2-year high in its final meeting of the year.
Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.86% to 57,499.16 while the Topix edged 0.11% higher to 3,750.4. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.82% to 8,763.8.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was up 1.52% in its last hour of trade, while mainland China's CSI 300 edged higher marginally, closing at 3,900.55.
SoftBank Group surged more than 7%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest rose 4.57%. Lasertec and Disco gained , while Tokyo Electron climbed 0.59%
In South Korea, memory chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics advanced more than 2% and 0.35%, respectively. The gains followed a bruising session Wednesday amid renewed concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending.
Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, labeled it a "solid day" for regional markets, suggesting investors were hunting for opportunities in the wake of an intense global sell-off.
"The rollercoaster stock market is back on an upwards path as a new round of Trump tariffs aren't as bad as feared and the US takes the day off to celebrate Thanksgiving," he said in a note on Thursday morning. "It was notable that investors cast their net wide for opportunities, fishing for bargains in the rubble following the tech sell-off and looking at other sectors in the quest for diversification."
But Mould warned investors not to be "too complacent."
"Oil prices heading higher is not good for efforts to tame inflation, neither is the prospect of retaliation by countries on the receiving end of new US tariffs," he said.
The Trump administration on Wednesday unveiled a fresh barrage of tariffs on more than a dozen trading partners, including China, the European Union and India.
Daniela Hathorn, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said in a Thursday note that the mood in markets was "cautious rather than uniformly negative."
"European markets are attempting to rebound after yesterday's decline, while U.S. cash markets are closed for Thanksgiving, limiting the chance to test whether Wall Street's late recovery can hold," she said. "The main focus now will be trying to determine how many further increases the Fed considers necessary in early 2027 and whether AI shares can withstand that rate path while investors continue to question the returns on heavy spending."
U.S. inflation data on Wednesday reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.7% in September, while core inflation came in slightly above expectations at 3.3%.
Mark Haefele, chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, said in a note on Thursday morning that his team believes investors should maintain strategic allocations to equities.
But he advised market participants to "review current allocations and use market moves as an opportunity to rebalance, refocus, and strengthen portfolio resilience."

articles.title_orig: Hamas weighs response after Israel kills 10 people in Gaza
articles.title_zh: Hamas weighs response after Israel kills 10 people in Gaza
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of Palestinians have been killed in Gaza in near daily air strikes over the past month
A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday.
Local sources told the BBC a residential apartment in Deir al-Balah was targeted at dawn, killing Khaled Abu Nada - the deputy education minister - and his wife, Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada.
A Hamas Civil Defence spokesman said that rescue teams and medical personnel had transferred eight bodies to Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza and Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.
In a joint statement, Israel's prime minister and defence minister said the operation was "part of a series of targeted killings" against Hamas officials.
Thursday's strikes also reportedly killed three Palestinians on al-Nafaq Street, east of Gaza City. Their identities have not yet been established, eyewitnesses said.
In a separate strike on Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, three Palestinians working for Hamas's security services were killed. They were identified as Yasser al-Lahham, Iyad Ahmed and Ibrahim al-Mashal.
Khaled Abu Nada and his wife Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada were killed in the air strike
In a post X, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the death of Khaled Abu Nada and said about 80 Hamas officials have been killed in the last month.
"No one in Hamas's leadership will succeed in evading us," he said, adding that the military would "continue to pursue our enemies and protect the security of Israeli civilians".
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had carried out a strike on a "senior" Hamas operative, and would provide further details later.
The attacks came a day after Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters were killed in Israeli air strike on their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.
On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.
Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,772 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he pressed Putin in China to pull back 'all military aggression' in Europe
articles.title_zh: Trump says he pressed Putin in China to pull back 'all military aggression' in Europe
articles.content_orig:

Donald Trump has claimed he urged Russian president Vladimir Putin to stop his aggression against Europe during their recent talks in China.
President Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday that he hoped Moscow would “pull back all military aggression against” unnamed “territories throughout Europe” in the hopes of making a deal to end the Ukraine war .
The conflict, approaching its five-year anniversary in February, has spilled over in recent months with drone incursions and cyber attacks that Europe has blamed on Russia. The Kremlin denies deliberately targeting Europe.
“I really believe this is a strong possibility — Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH — and will be a Great Tribute to everyone!” Trump wrote of a potential deal.
Trump and Nato chief Mark Rutte earlier issued a statement on the conflict, following a meeting at Mar-a-Lago on Wednesday.
They said they had discussed “the importance of Russia and Ukraine avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the War — and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the War, as rapidly as possible!”
The statement also touted the US’ investments into military equipment and munitions.
“Our “cupboard” will soon be full and, when it is, our Allies and Partners throughout the World will be benefitting greatly,” it read.
Ukraine’s general staff reported on Thursday that Russia had taken 2,091 casualties in the past day alone, reflecting a steady upward trend since 2022.
By comparison, Moscow was taking a mean average 415 casualties each day in October 2022; 709 in October 2023; 1,354 in October 2024; and 1,008 in October 2025, based on estimates from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
Ukraine assessed in September that Russia had taken 300,000 casualties so far this year - 18% of the casualties in 16% of the time since the invasion. On Tuesday, 24 November, the figure had risen to 432,519 casualties.
Western officials believe the toll is becoming unmanageable for Russia and in August estimated that the Kremlin was losing six thousand more troops per month than it was able to enlist.
US envoy and Trump son-in-law has given an alarming interview in which he shows he’s swallowed Russia’s propaganda - and worse - World Affairs Editor Sam Kiley explains:
Ukraine's military says it struck oil reservoirs at Russia's Transneft oil facility in Bashkortostan overnight.
The general staff says on Facebook that the military airfield Marinovka, in the Volgograd region, was also attacked.

A leak of 11 million death certificates collected from February 2022 to September 2026 suggests that Russia’s casualty rates have steadily increased over the duration of the war.
The information was initially obtained by the hacking groups Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow, who claimed to have obtained mortality data within dozens of terabytes of information from Rosstat.
The upward casualty rate seems to have peaked at 5,352 deaths per week in March of last year, according to the BBC, which notes delays in the reporting of deaths thereafter and incomplete data for 2026.
Around 325,000 troops may have been killed in the fiercely contested Donetsk region alone, according to a separate analysis by independent Russian outlet Agentstvo .
Fire broke out at Slavyansk ECO oil refinery in Russia's southern Krasnodar region after a drone attack, inflicting serious damage, the company said on social media on Thursday.
It said the attack took place during maintenance and stoppage which had been in place since a September drone strike.
Nearly 500,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in almost five years of war with Ukraine, according to confidential government figures leaked this week.
Data from the state statistics agency Rosstat shows that at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have been killed in the conflict since February 2022, according to analysis by the BBC.
The figures show how the invasion became the leading cause of death for 18-24 year olds in Russia, with 65% of those who died last year killed in the conflict.
It also sheds light on the monumental losses sustained to make limited advances into Ukraine, with some 20,000 soldiers dying for control of 10 villages with a total pre-war population under 12,000.
And the Ukrainian military estimates that Russia has now taken more than 1,643,000 casualties, including dead and wounded - more than three times the figure last reported by Kyiv.
Russia attacked two foreign cargo ships carrying more than 100,000 metric tons of grain overnight near Ukraine's Black Sea port of Odesa, Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi said on Thursday.
Koretskyi did not say where the grain originated nor where the vessels had loaded their cargo.
Ukraine has said grain shipments from its key Black Sea ports around Odesa have all but stopped since late July after Russia sharply intensified attacks on grain terminals and merchant vessels.
Russia says it does not attack civilian targets.
Ukraine’s charge d’affaires in the US Denys Sienik has said that restrictions affecting the operation of the Starshield satellite system in Ukraine remain unresolved, warning that the disruption could put civilians at further risk.
“The Starshield restrictions in Ukraine have created a vicious circle: neither of the key stakeholders has been able to clarify who made the decision to impose these limitations,” he wrote on X.
“The longer this situation remains unresolved, the greater the risk that it will gradually disappear from the attention of those who have the authority to address it. We cannot allow that to happen.
“To be frank and straightforward: Ukrainians already face enough life-threatening challenges as a result of Russia’s ongoing aggression. We cannot afford to accept the disruption of a critical service such as Starshield as just another episode and simply move on. This issue must remain on the agenda until it is fully resolved.”
He said: “The sudden restrictions, imposed without any prior warning more than a week ago, have placed Ukrainian civilians in additional danger. Every day these limitations remain in place creates real risks and potentially devastating consequences for people on the ground.”

articles.title_orig: Nvidia chip buyers told to rule out Chinese renters to buy GPUs, sources say
articles.title_zh: Nvidia chip buyers told to rule out Chinese renters to buy GPUs, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.
Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.
The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.
Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.
Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.
The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.
In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI , of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."
"For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said.
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries."
During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.

articles.title_orig: China and Brazil Lead Pushback Against Trump’s ‘Unacceptable’ Tariff Threats
articles.title_zh: China and Brazil Lead Pushback Against Trump’s ‘Unacceptable’ Tariff Threats
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks on reciprocal tariffs during an event at the White House on April 2, 2025.
China warned Thursday that it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” to retaliate against the Trump Administration’s proposed new tariffs , which have reignited global trade tensions.
“China urges the U.S. to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” said He Yadong, spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce. He added that Beijing “reserves the right to take necessary measures and will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”
The Trump Administration targeted 14 trading partners Wednesday in a slew of new tariffs that are set to come into effect early next year. The levies will be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 following an investigation led by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The U.S. said the probe had found demonstrations of unfair trade practices and excess manufacturing capacity. Mexico and Norway were not listed in the new proposals, as investigations into their respective trade practices are ongoing. Greer framed the tariffs as a way to “level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.” The Section 301 avenue is a way for the Trump Administration to reinstate many of the tariffs that were deemed illegal and struck down by the Supreme Court in February.
China is facing a 20% tariff, which the Trump Administration said it could double to 40% if Beijing does not adhere to the terms of an existing trade truce with Washington.
Another major U.S. trading partner, Vietnam, is facing tariffs of up to 35%. The country’s Ministry of Industry and Trade said it was in the process of “developing and submitting counter-arguments to the preliminary conclusions and inaccurate opinions and allegations from relevant parties.”
The proposed tariffs are subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing set to take place early next year before they go into effect, allowing countries to issue responses and arguments.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation, says the proposed measures are already generating significant “resentment” among trading partners.
On top of that, the proposed rates have prompted uncertainty for major economies as to what Washington could do next. “If the U.S. unilaterally determines that the partner is not living up to expectations, then the number can ramp up higher,” she says. “That doesn't really support trust, and it makes it very hard to plan ahead.”
Amid rising tensions, several trading partners are already following China’s lead in voicing their disapproval over the rates.
Bernd Lange, trade committee chair in the European Parliament, said it was “absurd” the E.U. is facing a 20% tariff. He expressed hope that any enforced tariffs will adhere to the Turnberry agreement signed between Washington and the E.U. last year, which capped U.S. tariffs at 15%.
“Washington’s allegations about E.U. industrial overcapacity are absurd. We’ll now see whether the announced U.S. tariffs comply with Turnberry in practice,” he said. “If Washington breaches its commitments, the E.U. must act swiftly. It has the legal means to do so.”
Elms says the threat to hike rates against economies that already have a trade pact with the U.S. further calls into question “how durable” trade commitments with Washington are.
Singapore and Japan also hit back at the prospect of respective 20% tariff rates.
Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade, and Industry said it was “very disappointed” by the assessment and argued that the U.S. Trade Representative’s findings “do not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy.” Japan’s Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara referred to the U.S. tariffs as “regrettable,” insisting that: “Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place.”
Alongside the sweeping tariffs against 14 trading partners, the Trump Administration published a separate proposal seeking to raise levies on Brazil by specifically targeting its sugar and aircraft exports.
“Imposing an additional, specific tariff on sugar imports from Brazil and an additional 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports from Brazil is intended to help bring Brazil to the table,” said the office of the USTR (U.S. Trade Representative). The announcement came amid stalled trade talks between Washington and Brazil.
The Brazilian government expressed “outrage” over the proposed raising of rates, arguing that it has “been acting in good faith in negotiations” relating to Section 301 with the U.S. for over a year.
“The USTR's unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the ongoing bilateral negotiation process. Brazil will not yield to this type of threat,” the government vowed in a statement.
It said Brazil would continue to negotiate with the U.S., “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products.”
The Trump Administration could face significant pushback from the U.S. Congress next year, as Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January following sweeping victories in the midterms.
Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will chair the Senate Finance Committee next year, has vowed to try and overturn Trump’s tariffs.
“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs, no matter the cost to American families, workers, and small businesses. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution,” Wyden said in a statement . “As incoming Finance Committee Chairman, I will use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariff chaos and restore Congress’ constitutional authority over trade.”
However, securing a veto-proof majority to rein in Trump’s authority could well prove difficult.
Among the general public, tariffs remain deeply unpopular with Americans. An NBC News exit poll following the midterm elections found that 66% of voters believed Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy.

articles.title_orig: Apple pulls Chinese-developed AI chatbot from App Store over reports of sexual messages to kids
articles.title_zh: Apple pulls Chinese-developed AI chatbot from App Store over reports of sexual messages to kids
articles.content_orig:
People walk past the Minimax booth during the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai, China, July 17, 2026. ( Reuters/Go Nakamura/File )
Apple has yanked an AI chatbot app with roughly 11 million monthly users from its App Store worldwide after reports alleged the platform’s virtual characters sent sexually inappropriate messages to children .
The app, Talkie, is developed by Shanghai-based MiniMax and was removed this week following Wednesday reports by Australia's ABC News and the United Kingdom's Bureau of Investigative Journalism that its AI-generated characters sent abusive messages to minors.
Although Talkie carries an 18+ rating on both the Apple App Store and Google Play Store and states that children aged under 14 or under 16 cannot sign up, depending on the country, child safety advocates have criticized its lax verification safeguards that allow users to self-report their age.
INSTAGRAM'S AI MAY CATCH TEENS LYING ABOUT THEIR AGE
MiniMax founder and CEO Yan Junjie, second from left, and COO Yun Yeyim, second from right, pose with Hong Kong Stock Exchange CEO Bonnie Chan, far left, and Chairman Carlson Tong at the Chinese artificial intelligence model developer's listing cerem (Reuters/Kane Wu / Reuters Photos)
Apple told FOX Business that the company enforces strict App Review Guidelines prohibiting offensive, sexual or pornographic material and previously took action against the platform.
Apple originally rejected Talkie: Personalized AI Chats in July 2023 for carrying a 13+ rating, requiring the developer to raise it to 18+ before launch. Apple later removed that app in December 2024 over objectionable user-generated content and subsequently pulled the developer's other app, Talkie Lab - AI Playground, for sexual content.
Apple also noted that as of Nov. 16, developers can declare whether their apps include "Dating and Relationships" features — which automatically triggers a minimum 18+ rating — with all apps required to complete those disclosures by Jan. 12, 2027. In Australia, Apple users must confirm they are 18 or older before downloading 18+-rated apps.
FOX Business has reached out to MiniMax for comment.
Launched in 2023, Talkie promotes itself with the tagline "Your dream chat partner awaits" and offers companions designed for sustained emotional engagement and human-like interactions, often with romantic undertones and immersive storylines.
Tama Leaver, an internet studies professor at Curtin University, told ABC News the platform's approach is particularly risky for young people still learning to navigate relationships.
"These tools really push on the edges of trying to keep young people engaging as much as possible, but there is no real sense of appropriateness in doing so," Leaver said. "It might be the case that a young person is actually investing quite heavily in the emotional landscape of… these apps and making themselves quite vulnerable."
An Apple App Store icon is displayed on a phone screen in this illustration photo taken in Krakow, Poland, on Jan. 29, 2023. (Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Together with its Chinese version, Xingye, Talkie generated over 60% of MiniMax's income in 2024 before the company stopped breaking out chatbot-related revenue shares this year.
AI IS CHANGING MODERN DATING, BUT EXPERTS WARN IT'S MAKING PEOPLE 'RELATIONALLY STUPID'
Other AI platforms have faced similar backlash over child safety this year. Elon Musk's Grok AI chatbot drew criticism from governments after it was used to create sexualized images of women and children , and AI companion maker Character.ai faces several U.S. lawsuits over its chatbots' inappropriate interactions with minors.
GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO BY CLICKING HERE
In July, China cracked down on domestic AI companion apps, including Xingye, banning intimate relationships for minors and ordering platforms to develop strict guardrails to curb emotional dependency and addiction risks.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
articles.title_zh: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
articles.content_orig:
The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation.
The airline said if no solution can be found, it intends to file for bankruptcy.
The airline uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo.
Prior to the suspension of flights, it was advertising services from London to Orlando, Cape Town, Bangkok and Phuket.
One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening.
The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic.
PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night.
In a statement on social media, PIA said all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet.
Londoner Fred was due to fly to Cape Town with Norse Atlantic next week for a friend's wedding, but has decided to change his plans.
"Yesterday the exact same flight I was going to get was cancelled, so I was worried" he told the BBC's Your Voice. "I sent an email to Norse and have had nothing back".
He decided to rebook with a different airline, which cost him an extra £1,000.
Another traveller, Claire from Herefordshire, is currently on holiday in South Africa with her daughter.
"We are due to fly home on Sunday and are now looking at a really expensive flight back," she said.
"We have tried contacting Norse but have been given an automated response saying someone will get back to us within three business days."
Consumer group Which? advised Norse Atlantic customers to not cancel their flights as the airline has not collapsed. Doing so removes passengers' right to a refund.
Rory Boland, Which? travel editor, said: "If Norse does go bust, whether you get a refund depends on how you booked and paid. If you booked directly with Norse, you may be able to claim a refund via your credit card provider, or possibly your debit card."
Those stuck abroad should contact insurers, while those with package holidays reliant on Norse Atlantic flights should contact their tour operator, he added.
Norse Atlantic Airways was set up in 2021 as a low-cost long-haul carrier.
It entered the market as a successor to Norwegian, which withdrew from long haul routes as a result of the Covid pandemic.
But it has struggled to make money, and its problems worsened this year, as fuel prices rocketed due to the war in Iran.
Unlike many other European carriers, Norse Atlantic does not hedge its fuel bills by buying supplies in advance at fixed prices.
This left it fully exposed when prices soared, with the cost of fuel roughly doubling at one point. Prices remain significantly higher than they were before the conflict began.
In the first half of the year Norse Atlantic made a loss of $94.6m.
In a statement to the Oslo Stock Exchange on Wednesday, the airline said its financial situation was critical, and it needed to find short term funding to continue its operations.
After suspending flights, the company said it was in discussions with investors regarding a possible takeover that "would include a financing solution".
However, it said if short term funding could not be found quickly, "it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy".
Norse Atlantic had been looking for a buyer since July.
Its potential collapse follows the failure of Spirit Airlines in May . The US-based low cost carrier was another airline left exposed when jet fuel prices soared, as US airlines typically do not hedge their purchases.
If Norse Atlantic were to fold, it would be another major setback for the low-cost long-haul model, which has typically proved popular with passengers but difficult to sustain financially, especially on transatlantic routes.
Additional reporting by Rozina Sini

articles.title_orig: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos set to lead European Central Bank
articles.title_zh: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos set to lead European Central Bank
articles.content_orig:
Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank next year.
He received backing from euro zone leaders at the European Council Summit, multiple media reported on Thursday.
The role still requires formal appointment after consultation with the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council, but neither has veto power and the decision follows intense political wrangling to reach a consensus on who should serve the eight-year term.
Reuters reported that de Cos was set for the nomination after the Netherlands agreed to back Klaas Knot, the only other candidate, citing European diplomatic sources.
De Cos is a 55-year-old economist and career central banker who rose through the ranks of the Bank of Spain, starting as a researcher in the 1990s and working in various departments before becoming governor from 2018 to June 2024.
He chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision from 2019 to 2024, and has been General Manager of the Basel-based Bank for International Settlements since July 2025.
Both de Cos and his main rival for the ECB top job, Knot, were widely seen as candidates with deep knowledge and experience in monetary policy and financial stability — attributes that took on particular importance at a time of resurgent inflation, fragmentation and political uncertainty.
Lagarde had extensive experience in financial institutions but was criticized by some early in her tenure for a lack of central banking experience.
De Cos gained sufficient political backing in closed-door discussions and negotiations since Lagarde said she would step down on Feb. 7, 2027, over seven years after she became the first woman to helm the ECB. That was despite a final push by the Netherlands at the European Council meeting this week backing Knot.
Representatives from the euro area's biggest economies — Germany, France, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands — have been horse-trading as they look to secure representation on the central bank's six-member Executive Board.
Influential roles as chief economist, expected to go to Germany's Markus Brunnermeier, and head of the Markets Portfolio, for which France's Laurence Boone has reportedly been tapped, also change hands in 2027.
Analysts say de Cos's commentary and actions over more than two decades at Spain's central bank paint him as moderately dovish — inclined to favor lower interest rates to support economic growth — but also as a pragmatist who has been willing to adapt.
That has included support for strong rate hikes during the energy price shock that followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but also giving staunch backing for rates below zero and the huge stimulus package launched by then-ECB President Mario Draghi to reboot the euro zone economy in 2019.
De Cos quipped in 2024 that he was an "owl" after being asked if he was a hawk or a dove, emphasizing his focus on data and the situation at hand.
"It is true that Hernández de Cos supported the ECB's uber-dovish monetary policy during the period when inflation was persistently below target. However, his monetary policy views may well be regime-dependent," Christian Kopf, head of fixed income and foreign exchange at Union Investment, said in emailed comments.
"We are now clearly in a higher-inflation regime, with core inflation in the euro area expected to remain above the ECB's target through 2029."
Kopf added that de Cos was the candidate with the "strongest technical understanding of monetary policy and central banking," which he said was important at a time when the world is "witnessing an assault on central bank independence, not only in the United States but also in countries such as Japan."
"By appointing a career technocrat such as Hernández de Cos as ECB President, the European Council would send a strong signal that Europe will not waver in its commitment to price stability and that the euro will remain a hard currency," Kopf said.
Spain's de Cos as president, Germany's Brunnermeier as chief economist and France's Boone as head of market operations represent a "carefully crafted package deal," Kopf also noted, because it balances representation from northern and southern European countries. The result was partially due to the knock-on effects of the German government pushing hard for the chief economist position, he said.
Along with a desire among politicians for influence, a north-south balance is seen as important as the northern countries are seen as leaning more hawkish — more inclined to opt for rate hikes and restrictive policy to tame inflation — while southern are perceived as more dovish.
John Orchard, chairman of the Digital Monetary Institute at think tank OMFIF, said that as a "central banker's central banker," de Cos had "managed to earn respect from typically hawkish northern observers."
Another supportive factor of de Cos's candidacy was the stellar growth rate of many of those southern economies in recent years.
Once the "sick men" of the euro area's 2010s sovereign debt crisis, Portugal, Italy , Spain and Greece have become some of the bloc's strongest growth drivers in recent years .
Factors such as strong tourism, relative political stability, increased foreign investment and strengthening public finances have boosted southern economies. Meanwhile, the euro zone's traditional powerhouse Germany has stuttered amid soaring industrial costs and a struggling autos market .
Orchard said that some believed that Lagarde's presidency had ushered in an "esprit de corps" at the ECB, with policymakers focused on the interests of the whole European economy.
That would, in theory, reduce the importance of nationality among leadership and of traditional notions of hawkish northern nations and dovish southern ones. However, Orchard also noted the recurrent theme of national representation in the recent debate and the perception of Knot as a hawkish choice.
Diverging performance is a core challenge for any leader of the ECB, which must set monetary policy for 21 economies all growing at different speeds and with their own domestic priorities and inflationary pressures.
But it has become particularly pressing this year as the bloc's second-biggest economy, France, is teetering on the edge of its own potential debt crisis .
Moves in French markets and whether the ECB needs to take more extreme measures beyond continuing to urge fiscal discipline will remain in focus for de Cos.
The ECB Executive Board's view of what measures could be taken to prevent market disorder and under what conditions was a key topic under discussion when choosing who should fill the roles, according to insiders.
Despite political efforts to pass a budget that will reduce its budget deficit to around 5% of GDP, investors have been driving up French borrowing costs on concerns over its mounting public debt-to-GDP ratio , high budget deficit and contracting economy .
Risks are being compounded by political uncertainty ahead of France's presidential election in April, which is stymying business activity and raising wider questions about EU unity as far-right and far-left candidates pull ahead.
Rising French yields and the widening spread in France's borrowing costs over Germany's have led to speculation over whether the ECB might need to deploy tools such as liquidity injections or its never-used Transmission Protection Instrument to protect other countries from contagion and support the euro.
This would be politically controversial unless France agreed to stringent fiscal discipline measures akin to those that southern nations signed up to during the Sovereign Debt Crisis — which could be complicated if far-right presidential frontrunner Marine Le Pen, who has a combative relationship with EU institutions, wins.

articles.title_orig: Net Migration to U.K. Falls to Lowest Level Since 1997, Excluding Pandemic
articles.title_zh: Net Migration to U.K. Falls to Lowest Level Since 1997, Excluding Pandemic
articles.content_orig:
Shabana Mahmood has just proved that the Home Office need not be a poisoned chalice for the ambitious politician.
She has every right to bask in the shower of praise she is sure to receive for having presided over the lowest level of net immigration since 1997 – 77,000 in the year to September 2026. For while she has built on reform initiatives by the previous Conservative government, the Home Secretary has resisted the basic instinct of her party to make it easier for "Third World" citizens to make their homes in the UK.
European freedom of movement ended when Britain left the EU and ever since, the civil service, aided enthusiastically by publicly funded NGOs, has tended to maintain six-figure net immigration levels by extending a warm British welcome to non-EU countries. This resulted in the disastrous "Boriswave" of nearly a million net arrivals in 2023 , more than a million in total , undermining the then government's claim that Brexit allowed us to "take back control" of our borders. That figure also turbo-charged support for explicitly anti-immigration parties such as Reform UK.
Mahmood is one of that rare breed of Labour MPs who understands that unlimited "open-door" immigration, as desired by many on the British Left, including her own party, is toxic to the progressive brand and a gift to the Right. Given the broken Tory promise that net immigration would be reduced to "tens of thousands" , it is extraordinary that this was finally achieved by a Labour government.
Still, the last government must be credited with starting the ball rolling on the reforms that have brought us to this point. It was under Rishi Sunak's government that greater restrictions were placed on overseas students bringing their families to the UK when they took up a university or college place (and it is reasonable to ask why on earth this was ever allowed in the first place; few UK students insist on taking their entire families to university with them).
Similarly, from March 2024, care workers were mostly prevented from bringing family members with them to the UK and a month later, the salary threshold for skilled worker visas was increased. It was the Labour government that, in July 2025, ended overseas recruitment for care workers and which again raised the salary threshold for skilled workers.
Mahmood has come in for criticism from some in her party for the reforms she has proposed to waiting times for applicants for indefinite leave to remain (ILR), a precursor to new arrivals being granted full citizenship. Stricter standards on applicants' proficiency in English, plus checks on outstanding tax liabilities and criminal records were also part of the Government's recent migration reforms.
But she has weathered the storm. Only 14 of her Labour colleagues voted against the Immigration and Asylum Bill at the second reading, confirming that, even if they are not particularly enthusiastic about lowering immigration, most Labour MPs recognise the necessity of it. Yes, Mahmood must share the credit for this impressive milestone in net immigration, but the rules of politics dictate that whoever is in the hot seat when good news arrives receives the plaudits. And she should.
There is always a sting in the tail, however. The number of people granted ILR has risen to its highest level in 15 years – 240,000. Ministers hope that this upwards trend will be partly reversed by the reforms contained in the new immigration legislation. Meanwhile, the number of people applying for British citizenship has reached a record high of roughly 320,000 , and the number of people granted citizenship – of whom Pakistani and Indian nationals are the largest groups – increased by 10 per cent to 265,000 – just below the record high reached in 2024.
The headline figures will be seen by the Labour leadership as vital to blunting the appeal of Reform UK and Restore Britain, and even the Conservatives. But Mahmood must be given much more freedom to continue her course of lowering net immigration, and that must include reversing the upward trend in grants of new citizenship. Otherwise Andy Burnham may find that come the next election, his party will once again find itself on the defensive, seeking to appeal to an electorate that has had enough of six-figure annual immigration.

articles.title_orig: The Canadian natural wonder created by a massive meteorite
articles.title_zh: The Canadian natural wonder created by a massive meteorite
articles.content_orig:
More than 200 million years ago, a 5km-wide meteorite smashed into modern-day Quebec. Now, this eerily perfect ring that's visible from space is part of an epic road trip.
Rain pelted my windshield as I steered northwards through the boreal forests of Quebec. Black spruce and balsam firs wove a dense tunnel around the road, and the sky was a low mass of clouds.
Behind me was the windswept coast of the St Lawrence River. Hours ahead lay an unblinking eye that gazes skyward – one so vast it's visible from space. Seen from above, the 72km (45-mile) wide Manicouagan crater forms an eerily perfect ring of water; mountains rise from its centre like a dusky pupil, while rivers and tributaries vein outward from the lake, vanishing deep in the woods.
Manicouagan – AKA: the "Eye of Quebec" – is one of the planet's best-preserved impact craters, created by a 5km- (3-mile-) wide meteorite that threw debris as far as Japan and may have wiped out entire pelagic ecosystems some 214 million years ago. Only when astronauts' photographs from space eventually appeared in 1983 did its vast scope become visible.
Until the 1960s the region surrounding the crater was roadless, but these days, you can drive there on a partially paved rural highway that forms the start of the 1,700km (1,056-mile) Expedition 51 road trip across Quebec and Labrador via the Trans-Labrador Highway, so named for the latitude it follows.
"For Québécois, driving to Manicouagan is the dream," said one local, whom I'd met earlier that summer near the US border. "If you're going, you need two things: a reliable four-wheel-drive truck and clear weather."
This was sensible advice. Yet by the time I filled up my aged and rusting Prius, a huge storm had formed in central Canada and was gaining momentum on an eastbound run. The satellite map showed violent rain showers barrelling directly towards Manicouagan. But it was summer and the eye was calling, so I left my home in Vermont and headed north.
The road to Manicouagan is Quebec Route 389, a two-lane sidewinder that begins in the city of Baie-Comeau on the north shore of the St Lawrence River. To get there I followed the river's coastline north-east 420km (261 miles) from Quebec City, a scenic drive known as the Route des Baleines (Whale Route).
As I drove, I scanned the water for some of the 13 species of cetaceans found in the St Lawrence River during its May-to-October whale-watching season – from slim harbour porpoises to immense blue whales. Standing on the free car ferry across the Saguenay River , I spotted an unmistakable flash of white.
"Belugas!" I cried, pointing to a trio of exuberant, melon-headed whales, which live here year-round – the world's southernmost beluga population .
At Baie-Comeau, I stopped to explore pink-streaked rock formations at Boisé de la Pointe St-Gilles park. Rosy snakes of feldspar wiggled across its waterfront slabs of dark-grey granite, which slope to the river's tidal flat.
The rain started gently as I turned north on Route 389, winding through S-turns to the hydroelectric dam Manic-2. In the summer months, the Hydro-Québec-operated facility – along with the bigger Manic-5, upstream – opens to the public for free guided tours .
Four dams were built on the Manicouagan River in a project that stretched from 1959 to 1970, my guide explained, as we walked through its growling inner workings. When water backed up behind the dams, the Manicouagan impact crater began to fill with water that swirled around the mountainous rise at its centre, creating the "eye" of water that's now visible from space.
"It took nine years for the crater to fill," the guide said, as we discussed the immense earthworks, blasting and engineering the barrages required.
Another 191km (119-mile) drive further to the north, mud-spackled trucks filled the car park at Manic-5, the world's largest multiple-arch-and-buttress dam, whose elegant concrete face seems to defy its massive scope.
I stopped for my second dam tour of the trip. In the surrounding valley, I learned, a temporary city sprang up in the 1960s to house workers, who harnessed the force of entire river systems. In the dam's small museum, I saw images of their families playing in the snow, heading to church, drinking at social halls. The project also brought roads here – including the one that would become Route 389.
"They did many things to build the dams, but what they did not do is ask the Innu first," said Céline Bacon, cultural and tourism officer for the First Nations Innu community of Pessamit, whose traditional territories include those covered by the reservoir.
Best time to visit: Snowmobilers and truckers journey to Manicouagan in the winter, but summer and autumn bring the best road-trip conditions. The Manic-2 and Manic-5 dams are open for tours from mid-June to the end of August.
What to do: Bring your own boat or paddleboard to explore Manicouagan Reservoir. Or, walk one of the trails into the nearby Monts-Groulx mountain range – like the 7km (4.3-mile) round-trip hike to the summit of Mont-Harfang.
Where to stay: Facilities at Manicouagan are limited. Relais-Gabriel at the crater's south-eastern edge offers very basic rooms and meals; the Innu-run Station Uapishka has a shoreline lodge, camping and meals.
The rain turned to a torrent as I continued north; dense stands of boreal forest crowded the edge of the road. For countless generations before the roads were built, Bacon explained, Innu people travelled on foot and by canoe into this landscape, returning each year to seasonal hunting and fishing camps.
"The dams transformed our territory, broke the ways we hunted and fished and gathered," said Bacon, who was raised on family stories of life on the land surrounding Manicouagan. "You can still see some of the old portage routes. My mother talked about them by name."
Rising waters weren't the only rupture. Beginning in the 1950s, Bacon said, the Canadian government increasingly forced Innu families to send their children to government schools, making traditional livelihoods impossible. "With that change, we lost so much of what we knew."
After visiting the dams, many travellers head south back to Baie-Comeau. Others go much farther north, following Route 389 to join the Trans-Labrador Highway to Labrador City.
"We've been planning this for years," said one visitor, from British Columbia, who was bound for the end of the road. He'd waited for retirement before tackling the journey. "When else do you have time for the Trans-Labrador?"
Compared with such trips, my own tempestuous, 11-hour drive from Quebec City to Manicouagan seemed restrained, an epic journey writ small. Yet when I caught my first glimpse of the rain-swollen reservoir, I was thrilled by my final destination.
A passing astronaut would have glimpsed only a thick quilt of fog; around me, saturated evergreens slumped, heavy with rain. I couldn't see much of the crater, but even through the mist the lake – the heart of Unesco's Manicouagan Uapishka Biosphere Reserve – conveyed enormous space and silence.
Scraping grit from boots sodden from that afternoon's hike to nearby Mont-Provencher , I checked into Station Uapishka , a lakeside research station and lodge operated by the Innu of Pessamit and co-founded in partnership with the Unesco reserve. Inside, I met Innu chef Simon Landry-Asselin, who prepares meals at the lodge using ingredients that he forages from the surrounding forest, like spruce tips and the aromatic leaves of Labrador tea, an evergreen shrub.
"This lodge is our chance to share some of who the Innu are with visitors," he explained. "It's my chance to share the ingredients that our ancestors have always known." That night, I dined on baked cod topped with fireweed blossoms Landry-Asselin gathered in the nearby mountains, as wet gusts buffeted the windows.
Yet the next morning, I woke to skies washed clear of clouds. When I walked to the edge of the water, I could see the dark summit of 952m (3,12

articles.title_orig: Spain’s far right hasn’t governed since Franco. Immigration fears could change that
articles.title_zh: Spain’s far right hasn’t governed since Franco. Immigration fears could change that
articles.content_orig:
Andalusia, Spain – Surrounded by shelves heaving with canned goods and cured meats, the owners of a family-run grocery store are locked in a debate about Spain’s upcoming elections.
All politicians are “liars”, proclaims 32-year-old Antonio Cerezo, announcing he will cast a blank ballot. His cousin, Patricia Nicolas Cerezo, 43, is less certain, riddled with doubt about who to support.
As for her 18-year-old son, first-time voter Alfonso Duque, the only choice is the far-right Vox party : “It can’t get worse than this”.
The one thing that the family in the small village of Rioja seems to agree on is that Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s socialists must go.
A former socialist bastion, the southern region’s political landscape has changed. Since May’s regional election, it has been governed by a coalition of the conservative People’s Party (PP) and Vox, once a fringe party that has drawn support by championing migrant deportations and tapping into a wider wave of far-right, anti-establishment support across Europe.
Ahead of Sunday’s snap vote, observers say Andalusia’s political dynamics could offer a glimpse of what might come next nationally.
That arrangement could soon be tested at the national level.
Opinion polls put the PP first, followed by Sanchez’s Socialists (PSOE), with Vox third.
The PP is projected to fall short of an outright majority, but together the two right-wing parties are expected to have enough seats to govern.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo has indicated that he would prefer to lead a minority government with Vox’s backing in parliament, while leaving open the possibility of a coalition like the one in Andalusia.
Tucked away between rows of greenhouses and arid mountains in the southern region of Andalusia, Rioja is home to about 1,600 people.
Overlooking the plains framing the quaint village is a giant silhouette of a bull. For much of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship , this area remained poor and largely agricultural.
As machines took over more of the work in the fields, many Andalusians left for jobs in industrial centres such as Barcelona and Madrid. In the mid-seventies, the Socialists found fertile ground in a society that had long felt marginalised and neglected.
In 1982, the PSOE won an absolute majority in Andalusia’s first regional election, beginning a stretch in power that lasted more than three decades.
But by 2018, the Socialists’ hold on the southern region was starting to crack.
A series of corruption scandals tarnished the party’s image, benefitting the PP. The PSOE still came first in that year’s regional election, but the conservatives took power with the backing of the liberal Ciudadanos and Vox.
“For the first time, the PP opened the door to the far-right to be able to govern – that created a precedent for everything that happens today nationwide,” said Bosco Govantes, political science associate professor at Sevilla’s Universidad Pablo de Olavide. “Before, there was a red line, a stigma, over collaborating with the far right. But that move in Andalusia kicked off the normalisation of Vox’s narrative.”
The party was founded in 2013 when a group of ultraconservatives, led by Santiago Abascal, broke up with the conservatives they accused of being too indulgent towards Catalan separatists.
Vox at first struggled to get into the political mainstream, but entered Andalusia’s regional parliament in 2018.
Once the Catalan issue faded from the national debate, the party shifted its focus to migration.
Abascal accuses Sanchez of enabling what he calls “a migrant invasion” to “replace the Spanish people” as the Socialist government adopted an open-door policy and legalised undocumented migrants who had worked in Spain for years.
Since the start of Sanchez’s rule to last year, the number of foreign-born residents in Spain rose from 6.3 million to 10.4 million, official figures show. He takes pride in the policy, as Spain’s GDP grew under his tenure.
Vox, the likely kingmaker that is expected to increase its vote share more than any other party compared with the 2023 elections, wants to reverse those policies.
Some observers say the conservative party has had to harden its discourse, such as calling for stricter measures against migrants, to stop haemorrhaging voters to its right.
Polling by Ipsos suggested up to 20 percent of Spaniards who voted for the PP in the 2023 elections intended to vote for Vox on Sunday.
Sanchez has pitched the election as a battle between progress and regression, warning that PP and Vox “only agree when it comes to cutting back rights”.
But that argument falls flat in parts of Andalusia, where some do not fear a Vox-PP deal.
“I don’t mind if Vox is in government,” said Rosaria, a 69-year-old retired housewife, while adjusting her white scarf with a red floral pattern. “The PP will keep them in check. It’s a party with vision and structure”.
Sanchez warns that Vox wants to roll back women’s rights.
The issue of gender violence divides the two parties.
Last year, the PP backed the renewal of Spain’s cross-party pact on gender-based violence.
Vox wants to repeal the 2004 gender-based violence law, which protects women from abuse by current or former partners. The party argues that the law discriminates against men and wants to replace it with legislation covering domestic violence regardless of the victim’s sex.
At an event against gender-based violence, Rioja’s PP mayor Olga Maria Gonzalez Jurado was asked how the two parties were getting on in government in Andalusia.
“I think it’s going well,” she said, but she deflected questions on whether the PP had hardened its stance on immigration to keep up with Vox.
In Andalusia, the two parties have been pushing for stricter housing rules for non-Spanish applicants.
Councils can already give people who live or work locally priority for subsidised housing, regardless of nationality. Last month, the two parties backed a non-binding motion urging Madrid to give Spanish citizens priority for subsidised housing and housing aid. Their regional coalition deal also pledges to give people with longstanding ties to Andalusia or Spain priority for public benefits and social housing.
In other regions, the two parties’ cooperation has reached classrooms and places of worship. Aragon dropped a school programme teaching Arabic and Moroccan culture this year and Andalusia is due to follow in 2027.
In the Murcia town of Jumilla, Muslims held Eid al-Fitr prayers in a car park after PP and Vox backed restrictions on the use of municipal sports facilities. The restrictions have drawn criticism over their impact on Muslim religious gatherings.
In Valencia, the parties backed a rule requiring meat served in school canteens to come from animals stunned before slaughter, which still allows halal meals that meet the requirement. In the Balearic Islands, they voted to send Spain’s Congress a bill to ban the burqa [full-face veils sometimes worn by Muslim women that hide the entire face, including eyes] and niqab [similar, but the eyes are visible] in public spaces.
Vox has called for the deportation of foreigners it says, among other grounds, also live on public benefits. This measure – to remove someone with a valid right to stay – has no equivalent in Europe.
The party’s policies have left migrants on edge.
Yudy Ramirez is from Colombia and entered Spain four years ago. For years, took care of her child while juggling two jobs as an in-house caregiver and fruit picker at a greenhouse in Almeria for five euros per hour.
In June, the 49-year-old finally received legal papers.
“Many of us are scared, because returning is not in the plans at the moment,” she said.
Still, not all migrants are targeted in the same way.
Vox’s rhetoric has an ethno-racial undertone which looks at Spanish-speaking foreigners coming from Latin America in more favourable terms as they belong to an Iberosphere which connects far-right movements in the Latin world whose centre is occupied by Vox.

articles.title_orig: iPhone 20 Pro Could Feature Ceramic in Limited-Edition Model
articles.title_zh: iPhone 20 Pro Could Feature Ceramic in Limited-Edition Model
articles.content_orig:
Apple could offer a limited-edition iPhone 20 Pro model that incorporates ceramic, according to the Chinese leaker known as Fixed Focus Digital.
In a post on Weibo , the leaker claimed to have gotten their hands on ceramic components for the 20th-anniversary iPhone, which is expected to launch next year. The leaker said that production capacity for the components is planned to be very low, suggesting they will be for a limited-edition model.
In a follow-up comment, the leaker claimed that the project would enter mass production if it passes engineering validation testing (EVT), and even joked that its scarcity could make it appreciate in value.
The leaker doesn't say what kind of ceramic components they have in their possession, leaving it unclear whether Apple is considering a ceramic rear panel, a larger section of the enclosure, or a smaller exterior part.
Apple already offers ceramic as a premium casing material on the Apple Watch Series 12, which comes in Pearl White and Night Blue ceramic alongside aluminum and titanium options. The company also previously sold ceramic Apple Watch Edition models, including a white ceramic version of the Series 5.
Interestingly, the ‌iPhone Air‌ features Ceramic Shield 2 on the front and Ceramic Shield on the back, and Fixed Focus Digital has previously said next year's iPhone 20 Pro models will use the same glass design , but with more pronounced curves along all four sides of a titanium frame. Ceramic Shield incorporates tiny ceramic crystals within a glass matrix, which preserves transparency while improving durability. However, the wording of the leaker's latest post suggests that ceramic could be applied in a more visually prominent way.
Apple's 20th-anniversary iPhone models are expected to launch in the fall of 2027 with a radical glass-centric redesign featuring a quad-curved display . Leakers have variously referred to the device as the "iPhone 20 Pro," but Apple's naming plans remain unclear. The company could well skip the iPhone 19 name to emphasize the anniversary, similar to when it introduced the iPhone X in 2017.

Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said on Thursday that two Italian workers were killed in Kuwait in an Iranian attack targeting a Kuwaiti military facility, according to the Italian news agency ANSA.
Speaking in the Italian Senate, Tajani said the drones targeted Kuwaiti military installations at around 2 p.m., including the facility where the two technicians were working.
"There was a powerful explosion and, unfortunately, according to the information reaching us from Kuwait, both of our fellow citizens have died," he said.
Earlier on Thursday, Kuwait's armed forces said several Iranian drones were intercepted, "causing shrapnel to fall and injure four people."
Kuwait's armed forces said several Iranian drones were intercepted Thursday in the small Persian Gulf nation's airspace, "causing shrapnel to fall and injure four people."
"The Iranian aggression targeted a vital site," the Kuwaiti Defense Ministry spokesman Staff Col. Saud Abdulaziz Al-Atwan said in a statement , without offering any further information about what had been targeted.
Al-Atwan identified the four people injured by falling debris as one Kuwaiti national, two Italians and one Pakistani national, and he said "the incident also caused material damage," again without any further detail.
The body of a Jordanian sailor who was reported missing after an Iranian attack on his vessel in the Strait of Hormuz last week was found off the coast of Ras Al Khaimah in the United Arab Emirates, Jordan's Foreign Ministry said on Thursday .
"The body of Mohamed Hossam al-Din al-Otaibi , may he rest in peace, was found on Wednesday," the ministry said.
The United Arab Emirates' state-owned ADNOC energy company reported the sailor missing last week after one of its vessels was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz. It said 11 crew members were injured in the attack.
The Jordanian ministry praised the efforts of UAE and Omani authorities for locating the sailor's body.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Thursday that two "non-compliant" oil tankers were on fire after striking sea mines while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz via southern shipping lanes the U.S. military insists are safe, but Tehran has repeatedly warned vessels to avoid.
"Since the early hours of today, two non-compliant oil tankers have exploded and caught fire after striking naval mines north of the port of Khasab," which is on the Omani coast in the center of the strait, Iranian state media quoted the IRGC as saying.
The report, which was not immediately corroborated by independent maritime agencies, said one of the ships was a supertanker laden with more than 2 million barrels of crude oil that was left burning after hitting a mine.
The statement — the latest in a series of daily claims by the Iranian regime of ships striking mines in the strait —   came after IRGC Navy commander Rear Adm. Ali Azmaei reiterated Tehran's warning to shipping firms that passage through the strait would only be safe "by respecting Iran's sovereignty."
"We not only have control of this waterway, but have also placed the power to change the equations at the heart of the Strait of Hormuz," declared Azmaei, whose remarks were also carried by state media.
Ship transits through the Strait of Hormuz have fallen again this month and the amount of crude oil and other products shipped outside the Persian Gulf remains at just over half of pre-war levels, according to data from shipping intelligence company Kpler.
The number of ships making the journey per week fell from 217 to 147 between Nov. 1 and Nov. 23, Kpler said in two reports this week.
Tanker crossings averaged 11 per day for the week ending Nov. 21, compared to 50 per day before the war, meanwhile, though the company noted that many crossings are "dark," or done with their AIS transmission systems turned off, usually for safety reasons.
The International Maritime Organization has recorded 141 attacks on commercial ships in and around the strait since the war began in February, including at least 15 in November. October was the worst month for attacks on vessels in the region since the war began, with at least 35 ships coming under attack according to the IMO.
The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations agency said late Wednesday that it had received a report of an explosion near a tanker about 50 nautical miles west of Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates, west of the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.
The tanker's master reported an explosion, which UKMTO attributed to an "unknown projectile," but the vessel was not damaged and there was no environmental impact, UKMTO said in an advisory .
Iran claimed earlier Wednesday, without offering evidence or details, that a liquefied natural gas carrier had struck a sea mine in the southern part of the strait — the latest in a series of similar daily claims.
Iran insists all vessels must use northern shipping lanes through the strait, and only with authorization from its military. The regime said Wednesday that it was tightening its control over the vital waterway, which the U.S. military insists is safe and open to traffic.
Yemen's Houthis said Wednesday they had targeted the Saudi ports of Jeddah and Jazan in response to Saudi strikes on a Yemeni port controlled by the Iran-backed group as their conflict further escalated.
The attacks came after the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said it had struck Yemen's Red Sea port city of Hodeida, drawing threats of retaliation from the Yemeni fighters.
"Both operations resulted in damage to the targeted sites," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said.
An explosion was later heard in Saudi capital Riyadh, according to an AFP journalist and residents, after authorities issued an alert warning of a "hostile aerial threat," which was lifted shortly after.
Residents in northern and eastern Riyadh confirmed hearing the blast, with one saying their house windows "shook violently."
Saudi forces said air defenses destroyed two ballistic missiles launched toward the capital by the Houthis, as well as a cruise missile in the western part of the country and a drone near Jeddah's port.
Turki al-Malki, the spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition battling the Houthis, said no civilian injuries resulted from the debris of the intercepted drone.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have launched a barrage at Saudi targets including the financial district, airports, energy infrastructure and military sites.
The Saudi coalition has in turn been striking Houthi-held areas of Yemen in support of the internationally recognized government, which has been battling the Houthis for territory since a civil war reignited in July.
The Iranian Foreign Ministry has called out Republican Sen. John Cornyn for a post on X criticizing Iran's alleged pursuit of nuclear weapons; however, the quote cited by the senator was actually about North Korean nuclear ambitions.
The Texas senator cited International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi raising concern "about a rapidly built extension at the Yongbyon gas centrifuge uranium enrichment plant."

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei correctly pointed out Grossi was speaking about Yongbyon, North Korea, and nothing to do with Iran.

The post on X remains live 24 hours after the senator shared it.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Halts Sales to Southeast Asia as U.S. Tightens China Restrictions
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Halts Sales to Southeast Asia as U.S. Tightens China Restrictions
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.
Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.
The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.
Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.
Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.
The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.
In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI , of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."
"For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said.
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries."
During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.
