articles.title_orig: From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices
articles.title_zh: From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices
articles.content_orig:
Ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working. Since its beginnings in 1998, Ars has never had a single, central office—a setup that makes for a great commute to work, with little risk of getting stuck in traffic.
As Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices. We’ve got all sorts of setups, tucked into basements, dens, spare bedrooms, apartment corners, and lofts. They run the gamut from minimalist “here’s my laptop and monitor” setups to “I really like collecting things.” Without any further ado, let’s dig in:
As an apartment dweller in New York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces. My current hodgepodge of equipment is probably on the minimal side compared to many members of the Ars team.
I’m usually multitasking on my basic monitor display and work laptop configuration, with the monitor sitting on a stack of several books (apologies in particular to Mary Beard’s excellent history of the Roman Republic, titled SPQR).
Accessories plugged into the work laptop include a simple Lekvey Ergonomic Mouse and a Logitech K380 keyboard that I’ve often brought along with me to public workspaces. Sometimes I’ll use the built-in Macbook Air keyboard, but I like having the laptop display elevated, whether I’m working at home or elsewhere.
My personal Apple M4 Macbook Air usually sits on the side, where I primarily use my old, battered pair of Sennheiser HD 518 headphones to listen to music during the work day.
I have a simple standing desk, but it’s not the easiest to change positions, so I wouldn’t recommend it for anyone who wants to adjust frequently. Whenever I’m sitting, I sometimes switch between a simple wooden chair from Ikea and a more ergonomic chair.
Aside from an assortment of coasters and a tea container turned pen holder, my desk also holds a painted dinosaur sculpture (courtesy of my young son) and two versions of the Spot It! Matching game (also for my son’s entertainment).
Last but not least, I have a pair of Powerblock dumbbells tucked under my work desk. I wouldn’t say they feature heavily in my work day, but they’re easily accessible if I have 15-20 minutes to spare.
Greetings from my basement hobbit hole! My desk sits across from a workbench area that was already here when we got the house. I have labeled drawers full of PC parts, tools, and cables accumulated over decades. The drawer organization was quite the upgrade over my previous solution of “chuck everything in unlabeled storage tubs.”
My current PC setup is an AceMagic W1 mini PC running Fedora, and a Blackview Intel N150 I keep on Windows for audio recording (PipeWire is fussy). The two are connected to my inputs and monitors via a KVM so I can switch back and forth at the press of a button.
The monitors are mismatched thrift finds. One is an HP, the other Sansui. The TV is a similar story—an old Samsung LCD that set me back $10 at the thrift store. I use it as a third monitor for watching PC streams. An Onn Android box is also connected, though it rarely earns its keep.
Below the TV sits a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, a repurposed B2B video-conference gadget modded to run LineageOS. It handles smart-home controls and tracks my solar production during the day. There’s also a Flashforge 5M printer in the corner, and the pegboard wall holds tools, Mega Man figures, and about 10 years’ worth of convention badges.
The back closet is the scary part: old consoles, spare drives, boards, and parts for every project I’ll get to “eventually.” The chair is a Dowinx gaming chair I grabbed on a Slickdeals whim—it’s fine, but I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone.
The rug-patterned Dude mousepad really ties the desk together, man.
I’m something of an outlier at Ars, in that I use Windows most days. I’m no great lover of Windows 11, but I still use it thanks to years of computing inertia. My machine is custom, built in early 2024 with a Raptor Lake Core i7 (that thankfully did not fall victim to the overvolting bug) and an RTX 4070 Ti. It has long been my preference to build my own PC for gaming and work to ensure easier repairs and upgrades. Although with the prices of components being what they are, I hope all these parts last a very long time.
The primary monitor on the bottom is an Alienware ultrawide OLED. I got it for gaming, but it’s also a nice productivity display that gives me lots of room to keep windows visible. Above that, I have an Asus ProArt LCD calibrated in sRGB for photography work. I’ll get to the keyboard, but I do want to point out my preferred mouse, a Logitech MX Vertical. I have carpal tunnel issues, and this thing has been a lifesaver.
I believe organizing my desk before taking the photo would be a form of lying, so rest assured this is what it looks like on an average day. I have a few organizers to keep phones and various accessories from getting scattered around my Uplift sit-stand desk (seen here in sitting mode), which I quite like. The chair is a Herman Miller Aeron, which I don’t like as much. It’s fine and has plenty of adjustments, but the mesh is very hard. You should only buy one on sale, and if you do, get a cushion.
Above the desk are some Star Trek cross-stitches, courtesy of my talented wife. The dangling ’90s-era computer components are a mobile I put together many years ago, featuring a neat Intel i486 DEC socket board and some SDRAM.
I’m not a particularly neat person. My natural state is to have two or three projects half-exploded all over every surface: piles of 3D-printed prototypes, spools of wire, a soldering iron, laser-cut acrylic for a pinball project, the packaging from something I recently opened and need to sort through. Those aren’t random examples; that’s the contents of my workbench behind me on the opposite wall of my office as I type this. It’s a bit of a mess.
To combat that tendency, I make a concerted effort to keep the desk where I spend so many hours of the day calm and a place where I can focus. It doesn’t always last! But I’m always at least striving for it, and what I find helps is having a very intentional design where everything has a place.
My desk surface is made from rubberwood butcher block, on Flexispot motorized legs. I recently picked up another rubberwood slab to build the cantilevered shelf. The supports neatly tuck away my M1 Max Mac Studio, which is still a great little workhorse with 64 gigs of RAM, and my Arturia audio interface, which I use to record line-in sources like synthesizers.
On the left is a task lamp and a pen holder with six discrete holes. This fits in with the intentional design part: I have to pick the six things I want handy, and I can’t just pack it with more and more stuff. Currently that’s my Apple Pencil, a Pentel mechanical pencil, an Olfa mini snap-off blade knife, and a selection of three Pigma Micron pens in different line widths.
The right side holds an Aiyima 10th anniversary hi-fi stack: A20 amp, D20 DAC, and T20 pre-amplifier. The speakers are SVS Ultra Evolution Nanos. They’re sitting on the latest version of some 3D-printed stands I’ve been designing. I print them with hollow legs and then fill them with concrete for mass and stability.
Since I know Ryan is going to flex on everyone with his keyboard collection, I have to try my best to keep up with my daily driver. It’s a Percent Canoe v2 case, running Holy Panda switches modified with 63 gram SPRiT springs for a slightly lighter touch, and GMK Bento keycaps. This was a pandemic build project, and it has served me well since.
I used to run multiple monitors, but I’ve found that I don’t focus as well with them and prefer a singular spot to pay attention to. I’m using an Apple Studio Display because I’m very picky about pixel density. I opted to order it without the stand so I can run it on an ergo arm.

articles.title_orig: Egypt tanker explosion kills 31 people as driver crashes into fuel truck in fiery highway crash
articles.title_zh: Egypt tanker explosion kills 31 people as driver crashes into fuel truck in fiery highway crash
articles.content_orig:
Cairo — A massive fire on an Egyptian highway killed 31 people and injured 21 others after a car slammed into a fuel tanker truck at high speed, Egypt's Public Prosecution office said Thursday.
The driver has been arrested, according to the statement. At least 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles, were destroyed in the fire.
The prosecutor said the suspect admitted causing the accident while driving around 70 miles per hour on a major highway in the Al-Warraq district of Giza, which is part of the Greater Cairo area.
The driver said he was changing lanes and overtaking vehicles when the front-left side of his car struck the rear-right side of the tanker, according to the prosecutor's statement, "causing the steering wheel to slip from his hands and his car to veer off course."
When the car hit the truck, one of the truck's tires exploded, causing it to overturn and slam into a concrete barrier.
Gasoline then leaked from the tanker and caught on fire. Images of the blaze on social media showed multiple vehicles on fire as flames and smoke billowed into the night sky.
The prosecutor said the suspect was being questioned to establish the circumstances of the accident and assess any criminal responsibility.
"It was a huge fire, the cars got stuck together because of the fire," Ahmed Sameer, who was stuck in traffic behind the accident, told The Associated Press. "It was a shocking scene."
Sameer told the AP he saw at least eight bodies being removed from charred vehicles.
Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi expressed his condolences to the victims of the crash.
In a statement on X , Egypt's health ministry said 39 ambulances took part in the rescue operation.
While fatal traffic accidents are common in Egypt, the sheer scale of the incident has prompted calls for greater accountability. Last year, nearly 6,000 people died in road traffic accidents across Egypt, according to official data.

articles.title_orig: Denny's brings back plaque celebrating Nvidia chief Jensen Huang
articles.title_zh: Denny's brings back plaque celebrating Nvidia chief Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia — and Denny's has a booth waiting for him.
The American diner chain welcomed the billionaire's return as Nvidia CEO by revealing that it had reinstated a commemorative plaque marking the birthplace of the artificial intelligence chip giant after learning of its removal on Nov. 13.
"Some things you just don't take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them," Denny's said in a post on X .
The plaque marks the booth at a Denny's restaurant in Silicon Valley, California, where Huang and his co-founders discussed the idea for Nvidia, which was founded in 1993.
The restaurant chain said it learned on Nov. 13, a day after Huang's resignation , that the plaque had been removed.
"We put the plaque right back up where it belongs," Denny's said, without specifying who had removed it or why.
Huang's ties to the diner chain, however, stretch back well before Nvidia's founding. He worked at Denny's as a teenager, washing dishes and serving customers before going on to build one of the world's most valuable companies.
The restaurant chain also disclosed that it had contacted Nvidia's communications team on Nov. 10 to express its pride in their shared history.
Huang's return came less than two weeks after his sudden resignation rattled investors and raised questions about corporate governance and succession planning at the chipmaker.
While his return has put those issues in the spotlight, Denny's offered a simpler message to its former employee.
"Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffee's on. We're always open, 24/7," the restaurant chain said.

articles.title_orig: US warns EU leaders against Big Tech tax
articles.title_zh: US warns EU leaders against Big Tech tax
articles.content_orig:
BRUSSELS — The Trump administration is warning EU leaders against taxing Big Tech as they gather in Brussels to consider new options to fund the bloc’s next budget.
“We oppose the EU proposal for an EU-wide digital levy just as we have opposed (and continue to oppose) other digital services taxes that discriminate against US companies while hurting consumers as well,” a spokesperson for the U.S. State Department told POLITICO in a statement, reiterating Washington’s years-long opposition .
European Council President António Costa on Saturday proposed reviving talks on a European digital tax to help finance the EU’s €2 trillion long-term budget and unlock a deal on its final size.
It would target companies with global turnover above €750 million, including at least €50 million in Europe — a threshold that would catch U.S. tech giants such as Google, Meta and Amazon.
The warning came as EU leaders opened a two-day extraordinary summit in Brussels on Thursday to grapple with the next budget’s complex funding equation: how much to spend and how to reduce the burden on national coffers by raising new revenue through so-called “own resources.”
The European Commission proposed an EU-wide digital tax in 2018, then shelved it to give talks brokered by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development time to reach a global deal . Countries such as France, Austria and Italy went ahead with national levies, drawing threats of retaliation from Trump’s first administration .
The idea of an EU-wide tax is now gaining traction again, with France, Denmark, Spain and Italy among the countries in favor. The push comes as Washington threatened new tariffs on the EU on Wednesday following a separate investigation into industrial overcapacity.
“This is a suitable area because the companies that would be subject to this contribution benefit enormously from the single market, and some of their activities and services are heavily undertaxed today,” an EU diplomat said Wednesday, briefing reporters ahead of the summit.
The diplomat dismissed concerns that the proposal could antagonize Washington.
“We cannot say that our American partner thinks about our feelings when it takes measures for itself,” they added, reporting “very little strong opposition” in the preliminary talks about the new proposal.
Ireland, Sweden, Malta, Germany and the Netherlands, however, remain cautious, according to three EU diplomats. Since a new EU tax would require unanimous approval, it’s still unlikely that Costa’s idea would fly.
But the German government will examine it “with an open mind,” according to an internal note seen by POLITICO.
“It must be clarified whether it can provide resources for the EU budget in a timely manner and thus contribute to solving the financing equation,” it says. The note also calls for clarity on “the international context.”
Leading the charge against the proposal, Taoiseach Micheál Martin repeated Ireland’s “strong opposition” to a digital tax. As he walked into the meeting of European leaders, he said such a levy “flies in the face” of the push for European competitiveness.
Tech lobby groups are also pushing back against the revived tax proposal. A coalition of 11 trade associations, including Brussels-based groups CCIA Europe, DOT Europe and ITI — whose members include the U.S. tech giants — warned Thursday that “digital services taxes have repeatedly triggered threats of retaliation measures from third countries.”
Thibault Krause and Pieter Haeck contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: At least 9 injured by large explosion and fire at major oil facility in Bangkok
articles.title_zh: At least 9 injured by large explosion and fire at major oil facility in Bangkok
articles.content_orig:
Watch: Fire and smoke billows out of refinery owned by energy company Bangchak Corporation
Nine people have been injured after an explosion at an oil refinery in Bangkok, authorities have said.
Three of them are in critical condition, according to news agency AFP, which said the local hospital had revised its earlier assessment of four.
A fire broke out after the blast at the Phra Khanong facility run by energy giant Bangchak Corporation in the east of Thailand's capital at around 14:45 (07:45 GMT).
The company said the fire was brought under control and put out within 30 minutes, adding that the cause of the incident was being investigated.
Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as local officials told residents to leave the area.
An alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.
Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery.
On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.
He said the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any issues.
Bangchak Corporation said air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges.
It confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.
An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

articles.title_orig: Trump's new tariffs would put rates right back where they were before the Supreme Court stepped in
articles.title_zh: Trump's new tariffs would put rates right back where they were before the Supreme Court stepped in
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
A new wave of tariffs from the White House would move overall rates almost exactly back to where they stood in early 2026, according to one initial analysis of the new duties.
The Yale Budget Lab says the newly unveiled plans , if enacted, would return the US to rates seen just before the Supreme Court struck down President Trump's blanket tariffs in February.
Read more: 5 ways to tariff-proof your finances
The estimated overall average statutory rate would rise from the current 11.4% to 13.9% early next year. The rate in February, just before the high court struck down Trump's tariffs enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977 (IEEPA), was 13.8%.
That remains well below the overall rates seen in 2025. The group estimates that 2025 rates exceeded 15%, peaking at nearly 23% in the weeks after "Liberation Day" in April 2025.
"The administration said it wanted to rebuild the IEEPA tariff regime using Section 301; with this proposal, it will have done so in the aggregate," the group said in its analysis.
The mix of countries bearing the duties will shift slightly, the budget lab noted, with apparel, electronics, and appliances among the biggest categories affected by the new duties.
The reaction from other corners, meanwhile, was that a combination of widespread exemptions, smaller rate changes on other trading partners, and many tariffs that will not be stacked meant the impact could be smaller.
"The latest US tariff announcement is not as alarming as it looks," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, wrote in an analysis.
"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices and keep core goods inflation firm into next year," he added, noting that an exact projection from his group will come later on.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer downplayed the macroeconomic effects in a CNBC appearance Wednesday, describing the total changes as moves that "really will just top up a few percentage points."
He added that the higher rates on China — the one place where the new tariffs are set to stack on top of other tariffs — are an exception and that the situation for most countries will be less dramatic.
One major trading partner dodged new tariffs this week when it was announced that an investigation in Mexico was still being reviewed. Greer added that recent talks have been going well.
Canada was also not subject to this eight-month investigation, which wrapped up this week and covered China, the European Union, and 14 other nations.
China is set for a 20% baseline "deal rate," which could jump to 40% if ongoing talks break down, while other partners will see much more modest changes.
Rates on some EU goods will jump from 10% to 15% if the new tariffs on excess structural capacity go forward and replace previous tariffs imposed around the issue of forced labor.
Yet the exemption for an array of goods that the EU and others enjoy includes key products such as semiconductors, as well as automobiles, steel, and aluminum, which are subject to a separate tariff authority.
Other goods the Trump administration has carved out in recent months, notably certain energy and food products, will also be exempted.
Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: Germany: 2 suspected Islamists arrested in Heidelberg and Cologne, suspected of plotting synagogue attack
articles.title_zh: Germany: 2 suspected Islamists arrested in Heidelberg and Cologne, suspected of plotting synagogue attack
articles.content_orig:
Germany 's federal prosecutor's office on Thursday said it had ordered the arrest of two Iraqi citizens in Germany who are believed to be members of a pro- Iranian terrorist group.
It identified the men as Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J., and said that they were arrested in Heidelberg in Baden-Württemberg in the southwest, and in Cologne , several hours' drive to the north.
Officers from Germany's federal criminal police force carried out the arrests.
Prosecutors also announced searches and raids of 17 sites in total across three separate states, saying these were ongoing.
Prosecutors said the two men were "strongly suspected" of membership in a domestic terrorist organization.
They said that Mostafa Al-R. wa an associate of a man in the US known as Mohammad Al-Saadi, who is accused of setting up a group with the acronym HAYI (Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya) that is thought to be "responsible for a series of attacks against US, Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe from March 2026," in the aftermath of the outbreak of Donald Trump's war with Iran .
Mostafa Al-R. and Al-Saadi allegedly "founded a separate organization to prepare and carry out further attacks in Germany and Europe at the end of 2025."
Prosecutors say Ameer J. joined this group. It gathered funds and "recruited several external people to carry out explosive attacks."
"On the group's orders, unknown assailants headed on two consecutive nights in late March 2026 — presumably with explosives — to synagogues in Cologne and in one other European city," prosecutors wrote. "The plan was, for reasons as yet unknown, ultimately not carried out."
Prosecutors said that intelligence behind the arrests could be traced back to the federal domestic intelligence agency , the BfV.
More than 250 police officers from various forces were part of Thursday's operation.
Both suspects were expected to appear before judges later on Thursday for a decision on them being placed in investigative detention.
One other person is being sought as part of the investigation, with several others not currently suspected of criminal offenses affected by it.
The stated date for the plot to attack Cologne's synagogue, late March this year, would have roughly coincided with a series of crimes in Europe targeting Jewish people or institutions in the weeks after the outbreak of war with Iran.
These included an explosion in front of Liege synagogue in Belgium on March 9 , which caused property damage but no injuries.
Police in the Netherlands investigated a fire at Rotterdam's synagogue a few days later . An explosive device was set off outside a Jewish school in Amsterdam soon after , prompting heightened security across the Netherlands.
In London, a Jewish ambulance service was targeted in arson attacks in March , not long before two Jewish men were stabbed in broad daylight in what investigators treated as a likely act of terrorism.
Several months later, in September, police in Wuppertal in Germany arrested an Afghan national on suspicion of trying to set a fire at the city's synagogue.

Fox News host Bret Baier has served President Donald Trump a humiliating Thanksgiving reality check on prices.
Speaking on Special Report on Wednesday, the host noted that the price of a festive meal for a family of 10 has shot up by 6 percent compared with last year, under the current administration. This ends three consecutive years of prices easing.
âYou have probably noticed that youâre paying more this Thanksgiving for your holiday meal,â Baier began, noting how âitâs costing about 6 percent more to feed your family this Turkey Day compared to a year ago, ending three straight years of price drops.â
He brought in Kelly Saberi from Fox Business, who broke down the costs and the reasons behind them.
Kelly Saberi gave a visual representation of the price surge.
âWe have a couple of reasons to blame,â she explained. âFirst of all, across the board, everything on the table, diesel and labor shortages are going to affect these prices. But with the bird, theyâve been facing three years of disease, and now theyâre catching up in the turkey industry. Also, there is a lot of demand for lean meat.â
Milk prices have climbed 8.6 percent, which Saberi attributed to âthe protein crazeâwe know everybody wants to get more and more protein in.â
Stuffing, sweet potatoes, and cranberries are all more expensive, while frozen pie crusts have dropped 2.7 percent.
âWe canât just have pie. I mean, you have to have the other stuff,â Baier responded.
Saberi said the price âfor this 10-person family that the Farm Bureau looks atâ is âup 6 percent since last year, which seems like a lot,â but when âadjusted for inflation it is 2 percent.â
Trump, a billionaire, has called the affordability crisis a âhoax.â
KEVIN LAMARQUE/Kevin Lamarque/REUTERS
âThey say the average for all the things on the table, which doesnât include mashed potatoes, I should note for people at home, will be about $56,â she added.
Thatâs below what Saberi said was the post-COVID ârecord highâ of $64 in 2022.
Ahead of the midterm elections, Baier wasnât afraid to warn Trump about what he thought would sway voters. âCosts,â he told viewers in an October broadcast.
âThatâs what this election has been about. If you look at the polls: higher costs,â he added.
It transpired that he was right, with voters opting for Democratic candidates in a massive blue wave.
Baier even corrected the presidentâs erroneous inflation numbers on his show.
Trump and first lady Melania Trump host the annual Thanksgiving turkey pardoning of two turkeys on Tuesday.
Tension between the pair boiled over in early November, after Donald Trump went on a tirade against the network. During a 23-minute on-air tirade, Trump aired frustrations about Foxâs pre-election polls , which showed his job approval rating at an abysmal 36 percent ahead of the vote.
âI read at Fox that Iâm not popular; the Fox polls are terrible. You oughta get yourself a better pollster because your polls are the worst,â Trump said.
But rather than let the dig slip through the cracks, longtime host Bret Baier, 56, confronted the president.
âBut tonight, actually, the results are pretty close to what the Fox polls showed,â Baier told Trump, the day after his midterm crashout.
Trump appeared to be taken aback by the pushback.
âWell, I donât know about that, I can just tell you about speaking for myself,â Trump said. âAnd, uhh, the results with Fox with me were wrong for 12 years; theyâve gotten me wrong for 12 years.â
The network has long aligned itself with Trumpâs agenda across his two terms. However, throughout Election Day, Trump made several critical Truth Social posts about the Rupert Murdoch-owned network.
He even implied that Fox News has been against him âfor yearsâ in one post .
âEvery question is a hit job and every answer is âBULLâ!ââ Trump wrote.

articles.title_orig: Trump Tried to Cripple Huawei. Now It Is Central to China’s A.I. Push.
articles.title_zh: Trump Tried to Cripple Huawei. Now It Is Central to China’s A.I. Push.
articles.content_orig:
China’s biggest technology firm and the world’s largest telecommunications equipment maker has been convicted in the U.S. of stealing trade secrets and defrauding banks about its business in Iran.
Huawei was found guilty on 10 of 12 counts by a jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday. The verdict all but brings to a close an almost eight-year-long criminal case against Huawei and three of its subsidiaries. The sprawling legal case spanned a 12-week trial, dozens of witnesses, and hundreds of motions and filings.
It’s a rare case of U.S. prosecutors securing a conviction against a foreign corporation and could have significant consequences for both Huawei and U.S.-China relations.
The Justice Department first announced charges against Huawei in January 2019 as part of the first-term Trump Administration’s “China Initiative,” a controversial program to investigate and prosecute Chinese influence and espionage in the U.S.
The Shenzhen-based tech giant was found guilty of bank and wire fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and violations of U.S. sanctions. It faces massive potential penalties, including fines, forfeiture, and restitution. Sentencing is set for September 2027, with motions in advance of sentencing expected to start in the third week of January.
“Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said .
James Barnacle Jr., assistant director in charge of the FBI’s New York office, added, “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.”
The jury, however, acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: racketeering conspiracy under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organisations Act (RICO).
Huawei’s attorney Brian Heberlig argued that U.S. prosecutors “began with guilt and worked backwards,” basing their claims of conspiracy on isolated incidents.
Huawei’s success, he said, is “about competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct.”
Heberlig told reporters that the company will appeal the case.
“We believe the government’s remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit,” Huawei said in a statement . “We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.”
Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig speaks to reporters outside federal court in Brooklyn, N.Y., on Nov. 24, 2026. Larry Neumeister—AP
Huawei was convicted of conspiracy to steal trade secrets from U.S. companies over two decades. Its alleged theft includes router source code from Cisco Systems, semiconductor equipment from CNEX Labs, robotic phone testing equipment from T-Mobile, antenna technology from Quintel, and networking equipment information from Fujitsu Network Communications. The jury also found Huawei and its subsidiaries guilty of violating the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and money laundering.
During the trial, which began Sept. 8, the jury watched a video that prosecutors said showed a Huawei engineer unbolting and detaching the arm of a high-speed T-Mobile testing robot and slipping it into his backpack. The engineer said he found the piece in his bag, calling the incident a “mistake,” and returned it the next day after T-Mobile reported it missing, but not before a visiting engineer from China allegedly measured and photographed the robotic arm, according to prosecutors. Huawei later fired the employee.
Prosecutors also argued that Huawei had hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by CNEX.
“Huawei cultivated a culture of crime and corruption, and that crime was an important business strategy,” U.S. prosecutor Taylor Stout said in his opening statement.
Huawei’s attorneys called 15 witnesses to give evidence that the company’s success came from its own innovation. The attorneys cited the company’s 110,000-person research and development team and its over 165,000 patents. Heberlig said prosecutors had “cherry-picked” instances of employee misconduct that were not representative of Huawei’s company culture.
Prosecutors also argued that Huawei deliberately deceived global banks, including HSBC, BNP Paribas, and Standard Chartered, about its business in Iran and North Korea, which are both subject to U.S. sanctions. Huawei allegedly presented its Iran subsidiary, Skycom Tech, as an independent entity to skirt sanctions.
The jury, however, rejected the government’s assertion that Huawei had conspired in a racketeering scheme to expand its global business. If the company had been convicted of the RICO charge, it could have faced potential forfeiture of parts of its enterprise.
“It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig, Huawei’s attorney, told reporters. The RICO charge, he said, “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge.”
The jury also acquitted the company of conspiring to obstruct a federal grand jury investigation.
The legal case is among the most extensive against a corporation, involving millions of documents in evidence, covering source code, financial records, and emails. Jurors spent five days, beginning Nov. 18, deliberating the case.
“Rarely has a jury had to commit so much of their personal time to a trial,” U.S. District Judge Ann Donnelly, who oversaw the case, said.
The case also took a winding path before the trial even began. It was delayed for years during the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2022, U.S. prosecutors also charged two Chinese intelligence officers with trying to bribe a U.S. government employee with $61,000 in bitcoin to steal evidence and information about the case.
The case could have ramifications on the U.S.’s relationship with China. The verdict comes days after President Donald Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. It also comes amid tensions over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy , which has renewed calls by U.S. lawmakers for tighter restrictions on A.I. chip sales to China .
Huawei, which is privately held, is one of China’s largest and most famous companies. The company reported 880.9 billion RMB ($126 billion) in revenue last year. It employs more than 200,000 employees globally and operates in more than 170 countries.
The case spawned a diplomatic crisis in 2018, when Canadian authorities detained Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou, who is also the daughter of the company’s founder, at the U.S.’s request. Meng had been secretly indicted on U.S. charges of bank and wire fraud.
Meng pleaded not guilty to criminal charges and fought extradition to the U.S. while under house arrest in Vancouver for nearly three years. She entered a deferred prosecution agreement in 2021, which acknowledged that she had misled an HSBC banker about Huawei’s relationship with Skycom, after which she returned to China. A federal judge dismissed the charges against her with prejudice in December 2022. The HSBC executive Meng had met with in 2013 testified in the Brooklyn trial.
The first charges were announced as Washington and Beijing were locked in a trade war.
Since the first-term Trump Administration launched the “China Initiative” in 2018, federal prosecutors have secured convictions against a number of foreign nationals, but corporate cases have had mixed outcomes. Taiwan’s United Microelectronics pleaded guilty to stealing trade secrets in 2020, and China’s Hytera Communications pleaded guilty to conspiring to steal trade secrets in 2025. Chinese chipmaker Fujian Jinhua was acquitted in 2024. A separate federal case in Seattle against two Huawei subsidiaries has been repeatedly delayed, with a trial date set for October

articles.title_orig: Recruiters Lured Brazilians to Fight Russia’s War, Then Stole Their Money
articles.title_zh: Recruiters Lured Brazilians to Fight Russia’s War, Then Stole Their Money
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine's " I Want to Live " project, which helps Russia's army servicemen surrender safely, published the results of an October 2026 survey of foreign nationals who fought for Russia under contract and are now prisoners of war. Hundreds of men from 54 countries took part, according to the project. The project posted the results on X .
Before signing their contracts, 49.2% said they knew they would fight against Ukraine and 14.8% said they were not sure. Another 28.0% said they did not know, and 13.8% said they were told something different. Only 1.7% said they were forced or coerced into signing.
The most common reason was Russian citizenship, at 46.7%. Next came being deceived about the nature of the job (20.9%), getting out of prison or avoiding prosecution (19.9%) and earning money (17.9%). Another 15.2% said they signed voluntarily to support Russia's actions, 11.6% wanted social payments and benefits, and 7.6% wanted to avoid deportation from Russia.
"I Want to Live" argued that a passport, money or freedom from prison amounts to a conscious deal and that claims of deception often appear only in captivity. Only 10.2% said they surrendered because they realized they had been deceived about taking part in the war. The most common reason for surrender was being wounded (48.8%).
After a prisoner exchange, 79.3% said they want to return to Russia and 18.1% to their home country. Asked if they plan to return to service in the Russian army, 13.3% said yes, 56.5% no and 30.3% did not know. The share wanting to return to Russia ranged from 96% among respondents from the Middle East and North Africa to 50% among Latin Americans.
The results differ sharply by region. Among respondents from Africa, 39% of the reasons given for signing were deception about the job, as were 24% among Latin Americans, compared with 10% to 14% in Central Asia, Asia and the Eastern Partnership countries and none among respondents from the Middle East and North Africa.
Who made the offer also varied. Among Latin Americans, 73% named an intermediary or recruiter. In Central Asia, Africa, Asia and the Eastern Partnership countries, a military enlistment office or recruitment center was the most common answer, at 40% to 48%.
Being wounded was the most common reason for surrender in every region except Latin America, ranging from 35% of answers in Asia to 48% in the Middle East and North Africa. Among Latin Americans it was only 18%, and the top reason was a lack of food, water and medical care (23%). Latin Americans were also the most likely to say they surrendered after realizing they had been deceived (15%), followed by Africans (13%), compared with 7% or less in Central Asia and the Eastern Partnership countries and none in Asia or the Middle East and North Africa. 19% of Africans and Asians each gave "I don't support the war against Ukraine" as a reason of their surrender.
On what they want after an exchange, respondents from the Middle East and North Africa chose returning to Russia overwhelmingly (96%), followed by Central Asia (82%), Asia (73%), the Eastern Partnership countries (69%), Africa (65%) and Latin America (50%). Latin Americans were the most likely to want to go home (30%), ahead of the Eastern Partnership countries (20%) and Africa (19%). Africa was the only region where 10% said they would stay in Ukraine. The project does not label values below 7% on its chart.
Foreign nationals lured into Russia's armed forces have an option to safely escape the battlefield with Ukraine's " I Want to Live " project. See our FAQ for recommendations for victims of Russian military recruitment and their families.

articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to
see more of our stories on Google.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and President Trump speak to reporters aboard Air Force One. Photo: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images
The Trump administration proposed a new round of tariffs targeting China, the European Union and 12 other economies over policies it says have created excess industrial capacity.
Why it matters: Trump officials are pressing ahead with his trade agenda despite a Democratic midterm sweep fueled by affordability concerns.
Driving the news: The tariffs are the result of  a trade investigation that launched in March , The proposed tariffs are a narrower approach than the sweeping import levies the administration has previously imposed, a senior U.S. official said.
Between the lines: The administration proposed tariffs of up to 20% to 35% on other targeted economies, though lower rates apply to trading partners with deals in place.
The big picture: The investigation was conducted under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The administration contends that foreign industrial policies encourage companies to produce more goods than global demand can absorb, undercutting U.S. manufacturers.
What they're saying: In response to reports of the proposed tariffs , China dismissed U.S. claims of industrial overcapacity as a "false proposition" and urged Washington to preserve stable trade relations.
Of note: The U.S. is also proposing tougher trade measures against Brazil, after imposing 25% tariffs in July over alleged unfair trade practices amid tensions between Trump and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
The bottom line: Trump's tariff agenda is moving forward as Democrats in the incoming Congress look to curb presidential authority over trade policy and lower Americans' costs .

articles.title_orig: MAGA splinters further over Trump's Nvidia shocker
articles.title_zh: MAGA splinters further over Trump's Nvidia shocker
articles.content_orig:
When Jensen Huang returned to lead the chip giant Nvidia this week after a scandal over his extramarital affairs, US President Donald Trump was not the only head of government to welcome his second coming.
Thousands of kilometres away, Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was celebrating too.
Huang once called Israel Nvidia’s “second home”, and Netanyahu reflected that feeling as he wrote on X: “Nvidia’s partnership with Israel’s tech sector has created enormous value for the company and for Israel’s innovation economy.”
“Continuity in Nvidia’s leadership is good news for that partnership and for the global AI industry,” Netanyahu added, referring to Huang’s reinstatement as CEO and president on Monday.
Global headlines have focused on Huang’s affairs, including with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset; his resignation’s implications for the AI industry; and the larger technology race between Washington and Beijing. His reinstatement at the company he cofounded has gone a long way to settle market jitters. Nvidia’s share price rocketed up by 30 percent on Monday.
But Huang’s return has also calmed nerves in Israel – arguably the country most impacted by Nvidia’s performance outside the United States as it hosts the US-based company’s largest overseas operations.
California-based Nvidia, the world’s most valuable semiconductor company with a market capitalisation of about $4 trillion, holds the key to the modern artificial intelligence revolution. Huang’s company holds an extraordinary near-90 percent share of the global market for GPUs – graphics processing units, which are specialised AI processors used in AI data centres.
Nvidia’s operations in Israel are its largest in research and development outside the US. It has doubled employees there in the past three years to 6,000 people across seven research and development centres in Yokne’am, Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, Ra’anana and Beersheba. It also has plans to build a major research and development campus in Kiryat Tivon near Haifa to accommodate up to 10,000 employees.
The Bank of Israel has estimated that Nvidia’s work in the country alone will add 2.2 percentage points of growth to Israel’s gross domestic product (GDP) in 2026, bringing it to 5.6 percent. Without Nvidia, that would be 3.4 percent growth, or 40 percent lower.
Next year, Nvidia is expected to add a further 2.4 percentage points to its GDP growth.
Nvidia paid about $1.29bn in taxes to Israel in its financial year that ended in January, according to its annual report. The company is projected to account for nearly 3 percent of Israel’s total state tax revenues in 2026, according to some estimates.
Huang’s resignation on November 12 initially rattled investors on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange (TASE) with the benchmark indices sliding after the announcement.
But by the end of the day, they had recovered. The TA-35 index finished 0.22 per cent higher at the close of the day while the broader TA-125 gained 0.07 per cent. The BlueTech Global Index, which tracks technology companies, fell 0.15 per cent.
The Haaretz newspaper reported, however, that officials at Israel’s Ministry of Finance were concerned about the potential consequences for the Israeli economy of turmoil – and particularly Huang’s exit – at Nvidia.
On Monday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog congratulated Huang on his return, noting “his deep appreciation to Huang for his continued support for Israel and for his commitment to strengthening the connection between Nvidia and Israel”.
Herzog’s office said Huang told the president that he was “moved by the message and that he intends to make the most of the second chance he has been given”.
Nvidia is helping fuel Israel’s economic machine during its genocidal war on Gaza, pogroms by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and the occupation of southern Lebanon.
But Israel is also returning strong numbers for the company.
The root of the tech giant’s relationship with the country can be traced back to Nvidia’s acquisition of Mellanox, an Israeli company that supplies computer networking products, in April 2020 for nearly $7bn. That acquisition was central to Nvidia’s success.
Nvidia was already able to make powerful engines that process AI workloads, but a single GPU cannot handle that workload and needs to exchange information with other GPUs.
Mellanox made the networking infrastructure that allows those engines to work together at a fast pace, creating the foundational structure of a data centre.
Nvidia’s networking business, built around Mellanox, generated more than $21bn in revenues in the third quarter of 2026. That’s about 18 percent of Nvidia’s total quarterly revenue.
At the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas in January, Huang spoke about Israel’s role in the development of key Nvidia chips.
“Nvidia’s BlueField-4 DPU and three networking components – the ConnectX-9 SuperNIC, NVLink 6 Switch and Spectrum-6 Ethernet Switch – all came out of Israel. So four out of six chips came out of Israel,” he said, praising the employees in Israel.
“Pretty amazing and maybe next time, six out of six chips,” Huang added.
A review by the American Friends Service Committee, a group that won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1947 partly for its work rescuing and providing relief to Jews during the Holocaust, has found that the Israeli military uses multiple Nvidia products.
Several purchases of Nvidia products were disclosed by the Israeli Ministry of Defence during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, a report by the group last year noted.
“They include products that are designed for AI applications, like Jetson cards and DGX,” it said, adding that since the public database only records unclassified contracts, “this likely represents only part of the full scale of the military’s usage of Nvidia products and services.”
Israel has made extensive use of AI systems in the Gaza war – including those known as The Gospel, Lavender and Where’s Daddy? – to track and target Palestinians at an unprecedented scale, the group said, adding that Nvidia “could therefore be potentially implicated in these war crimes”.
The Nvidia Jetson TX2 AI processor is also reportedly integrated into Elbit Systems’ Lanius drones, which Israel has used to kill Palestinian civilians in Gaza.

articles.title_orig: China firmly opposes proposed US Section 301 tariffs
articles.title_zh: China firmly opposes proposed US Section 301 tariffs
articles.content_orig:
China on Thursday said it firmly opposes proposed US Section 301 tariffs on imports from 14 economies, including China, and urged Washington to correct its course and resolve the issue through dialogue and consultation.
Speaking at a news conference in Beijing, Ministry of Commerce spokesman He Yadong said China would closely follow developments and reserve the right to take necessary measures to safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.
He described the US investigations as “a typical act of unilateralism”, saying they seriously undermine the international economic order and violate World Trade Organization rules.
ALSO READ: China's high-tech FDI surges 31.3% in first 10 months
The Office of the US Trade Representative on Nov 25 released the findings of its investigations into alleged manufacturing overcapacity and proposed additional tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
“Some countries are pursuing protectionism in the name of addressing overcapacity, politicizing normal market competition and turning industrial development issues into political tools,” He said.
He said such measures would leave those countries’ structural problems unresolved, destabilize global industrial and supply chains, disrupt industrial cooperation and push up global inflation.
They would also harm businesses and consumers and pose long-term, systemic risks to global economic growth, he added.
On July 28, the Ministry of Commerce released a position paper on so-called overcapacity, calling for a comprehensive and objective assessment of global industrial capacity and for greater international cooperation.

articles.title_orig: U.S. chip curbs and distillation crackdown to impact Chinese AI model progress
articles.title_zh: U.S. chip curbs and distillation crackdown to impact Chinese AI model progress
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.
Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.
The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.
Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.
Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.
The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.
In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI , of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."
"For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said.
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries."
During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.

articles.title_orig: Shein agrees to pay $100 million to settle claims of misleading customers
articles.title_zh: Shein agrees to pay $100 million to settle claims of misleading customers
articles.content_orig:
Fast-fashion retailer Shein has agreed to pay $100 million to settle Federal Trade Commission allegations that it misled customers.
The FTC says the money will be used to compensate customers harmed by the company's practices.
The agency said tens of thousands of customers reported receiving their orders late, while others never received them at all. Shein allegedly failed to notify customers of shipping delays as required by law.
RELATED STORY | Fashion giant Shein facing new scrutiny from US regulators
The FTC also accused Shein of publishing positive product reviews while suppressing or deleting negative ones.
Investigators also found that some cotton Shein advertised as U.S.-grown originated in China.
Under the proposed settlement, Shein would be required to stop misrepresenting delivery times, suppressing negative reviews and making deceptive claims about its supply chain. The company would also have to provide adequate customer service.

articles.title_orig: U.S. tariff-hike threats pile pressure on partners to sign trade deals
articles.title_zh: U.S. tariff-hike threats pile pressure on partners to sign trade deals
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration has unveiled a fresh tariff salvo on more than a dozen trading partners, with China, Vietnam, and India facing some of the steepest potential rates and mounting pressure to conclude trade deals with Washington.
The proposed tariffs, framed as curbing excess industrial capacity, start at 15% for the European Union, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan and rise to as much as 35% for Vietnam.
The U.S. Trade Representative's Office said it intends to cap the new duties at lower levels for countries that have completed trade deals or are still negotiating with Washington.
The overall impact on the region is likely to be limited, said Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics. The proposal "puts most of the targeted countries back where they were earlier in the year," he said, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's emergency tariffs in February.
Still, the proposal could give some countries an incentive to speed up trade talks in order to lock in lower tariff rates, analysts said.
On Wednesday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the new policy likely will not take effect for months, with a senior U.S. official saying the duties could take effect as early as January.
China faces a capped rate of 20%, on top of an existing 25% tariff imposed during President Donald Trump's first term. The rate could rise to 40% if the trade truce reached in South Korea last October is not extended beyond January, the USTR said.
Beijing has rejected Washington's claim of excess capacity while vowing to take measures necessary to protect its rights.
On Thursday, Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yadong called on Washington to "rectify its wrongdoing and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue."
He was responding to Washington's plan to raise tariffs following its Section 301 investigations, while the ministry also urged the U.S. to implement $30 billion of reciprocal tariff cuts agreed by the two sides in late September.
The renewed tensions come despite several conciliatory meetings between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping this year, as well as what Williams described as Trump's "apparent lack of concern" about allegations that Chinese technology firms have circumvented U.S. chip export controls.
The two leaders are expected to meet for a fourth time this year at the Group of 20 leaders summit in Miami in December.
"While not happy, Beijing seems prepared to live with the new rates provided that they don't exceed 20%," said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
By retaining the option to raise levies if bilateral talks deteriorate, Washington is using the tariffs as leverage to "secure expected shipments of critical minerals and rare earths, and further purchases of U.S. agricultural goods," Cutler said.
Washington has warned that tariffs on Chinese goods could double to 40% if the USTR finds that Beijing is not engaging. "If the trade war did start up again, today's measures provide the U.S. with some ammunition," Williams said.
Even the sweeping actions against the other 13 trading partners appear aimed squarely at China, said Williams, who tallied that the word "China" appears 253 times in the USTR's report on Vietnam, and 315 times in the document on the European Union.
"Foremost among the 'unreasonable acts, policies, and practices' that these countries are criticised for is being slow to restrict imports and FDI from China," Williams said.
While the proposed tariffs generally lift average rates only modestly, India and Vietnam stand out because of the wider gaps between the rates they would face with and without a deal, analysts said.
India and Vietnam face proposed tariffs of 25% and 35%, respectively, but those rates could fall sharply to 17% and 20% if ongoing talks with the U.S. produce reciprocal trade agreements.
The two countries have "a strong incentive" to conclude deals with Washington to secure the lower rates, Cutler said.
Vietnam's trade ministry said Thursday that it was working with the U.S. to complete a trade deal as soon as possible, according to Reuters . India could also gain an edge over some Asian rivals through comparatively lower levies if New Delhi concludes its long-pending trade deal with Washington.
Singapore faces a similar challenge. The proposal sets a maximum potential rate of 20% on its exports, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, which could fall to 10% if it reaches an agreement on reciprocal trade with the U.S. or concludes other negotiations addressing the USTR's findings, according to Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry .
The ministry said it disagreed with the findings and was "very disappointed" with the proposed action, arguing that it failed to account for the structure of Singapore's economy.
Under the U.S.-Singapore Free Trade Agreement, Singapore imposes zero tariffs on U.S. goods, while the U.S. has run a trade surplus with the city-state for more than 20 years, the ministry said. That surplus grew to $33 billion in 2025 from $27 billion in 2024.
Singapore said it would submit further comments during the public consultation period and urge the USTR to reconsider.
Exemptions for semiconductors and other electronics should cushion the impact on South Korea and Taiwan, whose economies are heavily concentrated in those sectors, analysts said.
The USTR singled out South Korea for its concentration in memory-chip production and what it described as outsized government support. Yet it excluded the country's chips from the proposed excess-capacity tariffs.
Taiwan, which faces an excess-capacity tariff cap of 15%, also benefits from exemptions for other electronics, including mobile phones and networking equipment. Its effective tariff rate would rise to about 9% from 6%, Williams estimated.
— CNBC's Evelyn Cheng contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: FedEx plane overshoots Miami runway, causing brief suspension of flights at airport
articles.title_zh: FedEx plane overshoots Miami runway, causing brief suspension of flights at airport
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) temporarily halted flights bound for Miami International Airport in Florida after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway on Wednesday evening.
Departures heading to Miami were grounded just after 20:15 local time (01:15 GMT) and all but one runway at the airport was closed, according to the FAA advisory. Flights resumed again about 90 minutes later.
The airliner that ran past the runway arrived from Memphis. No injuries have been reported. The FAA is investigating the incident.
The ground stop came on the day before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel days of the year in the US.
Flight delays in Miami reached one hour but appeared to be declining later Wednesday night.
At 21:41 local time, the FAA confirmed that "flights will be resuming shortly".
Passengers scheduled to travel on Wednesday night were encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport.
"We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations," Miami-Dade Aviation Department spokesman Greg Chin said in a statement to the BBC.
The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travellers in the country over this holiday week, according to the American Automobile Association.
The Miami-Dade area is also under a flood watch until late Wednesday night. Periods of heavy rain throughout the day are expected to cause flooding, according to the US National Weather Service.
A nationwide ground stop earlier this month halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.

articles.title_orig: A Chinese consumer advocate is stranded in South Korea as a crackdown in China targets campaigners
articles.title_zh: A Chinese consumer advocate is stranded in South Korea as a crackdown in China targets campaigners
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Chinese consumer rights advocate Wang Hai has spent three decades exposing counterfeit goods and seeking compensation for buyers. In recent months, he left China fearing he was a target of the authorities, but now he is stranded in South Korea with his family, facing possible deportation home.
Wang, a well-known campaigner against counterfeit goods, said China invalidated his passport and South Korean authorities rejected his asylum. The United States also revoked his tourist visa, narrowing his options for leaving South Korea and deepening his fears of being sent back to China.
Chinese authorities launched a campaign against organized crime in July, saying they would target “malicious compensation claims.” Since then, authorities have arrested at least 100 people for allegedly extorting businesses through anti-counterfeiting work or consumer compensation claims, according to official statements reviewed by The Associated Press.
Wang said the arrests made him fear he could be next, prompting him to leave a country where official Chinese media had once praised him for his role as anti-counterfeiting activist.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs told The Associated Press it was not aware of Wang’s case. The Ministry of Public Security did not respond to a request for comment.
The quagmire in which Wang, 53, and his family have found themselves has drawn concerns from rights advocates over China’s efforts to target critics abroad and the narrowing options for people seeking refuge in the U.S.
“The Chinese government’s practice of transnational repression is well documented, including in South Korea,” said Yaqiu Wang, senior China researcher at Human Rights Watch, based in Washington , and “there is no doubt that the Trump administration has created a far more hostile environment for immigrants, and even visitors.”
Wang spoke to the AP from South Korea about his situation and has appealed the rejection of his asylum application in that country.
The activist fears he will end up in jail if deported to China
The activist said that he arrived in South Korea in late September with his wife, 8-year-old daughter and infant son.
Wang said he believed Chinese authorities were targeting him and that dozens of his staff members were arrested and questioned. Some remain in detention, he said. One staffer had his passport revoked while traveling from Thailand to Singapore last month, according to him.
“The very same job has suddenly morphed from being praised into something associated with organized crime — it’s absolutely surreal," said Wang.
Asked what he is afraid of if he is sent to China, Wang didn’t hesitate: “I would definitely spend the rest of my life behind bars.”
A notice reviewed by AP showed South Korean immigration authorities rejected Wang's and his family's applications for refugee status. AP also reviewed the U.S. Embassy email that revoked his visa, in which U.S. authorities told Wang that new information made him inadmissible to the U.S. or ineligible for a U.S. visa but did not provide specific details.
The U.S. State Department didn't immediately respond to the request for comment.
He was once praised as a ‘woodpecker’ rooting out fraud
Wang became a household name in China in the 1990s for exposing counterfeit goods, an increasingly widespread problem as the country’s market economy expanded rapidly and consumer protection oversight lagged.
In 1998, Wang joined a roundtable discussion with then-U.S. President Bill Clinton during his visit to Shanghai. Wang told Clinton he had been viewed as “immoral” at home, according to a White House transcript.
Chinese state media, however, largely portrayed him favorably, calling him “China’s No. 1 anti-counterfeiting activist.” Professional consumer advocates were compared to “woodpeckers,” rooting out problems in the marketplace.
Wang ran a rights-protection company in Beijing for about 30 years and a testing laboratory supporting anti-counterfeiting work for five years. He said both were forced to close after many of his staff, including three lawyers, were arrested in September.
The closure of his offices came after China launched its campaign against organized crime. Authorities said some people were using consumer complaints, lawsuits or threats of exposure to extort money from businesses through what officials called “malicious compensation claims.”
Some lawyers say consumer rights advocates play a positive role by exposing illegal practices, pressing businesses to address problems and helping authorities enforce regulations.
“The fact that some individuals engage in these activities as a profession or as a source of income does not invalidate the legitimacy of such social oversight itself,” said Zhang Yansheng, a Beijing-based lawyer.
After fleeing China, Wang seeks a new home with freedom
Wang’s consumer advocacy began more than three decades ago, when he suspected two pairs of Sony headphones he bought at a Beijing department store were counterfeit. He bought the remaining 10 pairs and secured compensation of twice the purchase price. It was widely celebrated on Chinese state media as a pioneering case of consumer activism.
He went on to run his own company and testing lab, helping consumers seek compensation and pushing for stronger consumer protections.
Wang and other advocates also pushed for a minimum compensation payment of 500 yuan ($75) for consumers, a proposal later incorporated into a revised consumer protection law in 2013.
His most recent case involved helping cherry farmers in the northeastern city of Dalian get compensation after they bought fake pesticide. He said Dalian police later arrested and detained around four dozens of people including the cherry farmers, two lawyers who represented the farmers, and Wang's staff.
Wang said he has since focused on researching asylum options and hopes to settle in the U.S., Canada, Britain, Australia or New Zealand, seeking what he called “real law enforcement and freedom” to “get away from China's transnational repression.”
After his U.S. visa was revoked, Wang is seeking resettlement in Canada with the help of a human rights organization.
Fearing arrest by Chinese authorities even outside China, he said he and his family mostly stay indoors in South Korea. He said his bank accounts in China have been frozen, leaving the family in financial difficulty, and his 8-year-old daughter is struggling with her mental health because she cannot attend school.

It's not a new deal (it's been running for a few days now) but the Nintendo Switch 2 + Mario Kart World bundle for $499 is the biggest deal of Black Friday by far if you ask me. Also, while the big new holiday title, The Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time, isn't discounted, you can save $12 on The Legend of Zelda Breath of the Wild .
Stay tuned for all the best Black Friday Nintendo Switch deals live.
Nintendo's Black Friday sale has arrived! For $499, you can pick up a Nintendo Switch 2 bundle that includes the console, Mario Kart World and a three-month Nintendo Switch Online membership. That's an $87 saving compared to purchasing each item individually. The deal also brings the bundle back to its original launch price, before the Switch 2's price increase. While it's not a brand-new discount, it's still a pretty compelling offer, particularly when you consider the rising prices of competing consoles like the PS5 and Xbox.
The biggest game on the Switch 2 right now is undoubtedly The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Right now, there's a teeny-tiny, fairy-sized discount on Link's remastered adventure over at Amazon. The full price is $59, but you can get $5 off the digital version by adding it to your cart right now.
I know, I know — $5 isn't going to shake the foundations of Hyrule Castle, but this is the best Nintendo Switch 2 game available right now, so any rupees saved are a bonus, right?
One of the best selling Nintendo Switch 2 accessories for Black Friday is this 256GB Samsung P9 microSD card. It adds 256GB of extra space for your digital games, save data and screenshots. Unfortunately, it's not at its lowest price ever (it sold for $31 back in March,) but storage prices are generally on the rise. Buying now is a good idea because it might be the lowest price we see for a long time.
If you don't like how your Joy-Con 2's thumbsticks feel, you can get a grip on the situation with these grips from Jsaux! These come with a set of three different size grips, so you can experiment with what you like best and get the perfect feel. As well as protecting your controller's original thumbsticks, they can also help you aim and move the sticks more precisely!
There are lots of Castlevania-inspired games out there, but nothing beats the original series! If you're ready to dive in, you can get $10 off Castlevania Belmont's Curse over at Best Buy right now. Castlevania's whip is absolutely iconic to the franchise and this time around, it's not just a weapon — you can also use it to increase your movement options. You'll need to explore a ton of spooky hallways and master the game's tricky combat system to complete this game. Plus, just look at that gorgeous art style!
Konami just dropped a bunch of new Black Friday discounts on Amazon! They're well known for their Silent Hill and Castlevania series, but I think the deal Nintendo fans should pay attention to is on Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Volume 2 . My colleague Tony Polanco checked out the game on PS5 and called it "an almost perfect port of [his] favorite PS3 exclusive." This essential spy thriller stealth game can finally be played on platforms other than PS3, and it has been enhanced with improved visuals and way, way faster loading times!
If you need to catch up on Metal Gear, you can also grab Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol. 1 for $36 at Walmart .

Despite being so affordable, it comes with some handy features like a play stand for tabletop gaming sessions, and game card cases that fit in under to console with space for 8 game cartridges. It's a popular buy on Amazon, with reviewers confirming that it holds up well even after years of use.
Yes, you read that right. Mario Kart 8 Deluxe is the best selling Nintendo Switch game ever with 72 million copies sold, and now you can get a copy for just $40 ($19 less than full price.) Although Mario Kart World is out now, there are still plenty of reasons to pick up MK8D. For starters, it's a lot cheaper than Mario Kart World's $79 asking price. It still provides a ton of fun and has 48 iconic tracks to race on. And what's more, Mario Kart 8 Deluxe had crossovers with other Nintendo franchises, meaning you can play as characters from The Legend of Zelda, Animal Crossing and Splatoon.

This 3D platformer is simply incredible, offering a huge, unique world to explore, with near countless exciting challenges and secrets to discover. It's arguably Mario's biggest and best adventure yet.
And it's not just me who loves it — we gave Super Mario Odyssey 4.5-stars in our review and it currently sits at the #2 spot on our list of the best Nintendo Switch games . If you still haven't played it, now is the time to change that as it's on sale for 20% off over at Walmart.

There are a ton of classic arcade games to choose from on Switch, from Street Fighter to Tetris, and if you love the feel of a classic button-only controller, this is a great one to pick up. SpaceX announced Wednesday that it will contribute one share of its stock to every currently active Trump Account, with CEO Elon Musk pledging to personally match the company's donation.
The aerospace company's commitment follows Musk's pledge earlier this year to give every child in America a share of the company.
Musk elaborated on the planned stock giveaway in a post on X Wednesday evening, saying every child in America would receive an additional share from him personally.
"Every child in America will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from me personally," Musk wrote.
TRUMP ACCOUNTS HIT MAJOR MILESTONE AS FAMILY CONTRIBUTIONS SURPASS $1 BILLION
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pledged to personally match the company's planned donation of one share of stock to every currently active Trump Account. (Getty Images)
SpaceX said the planned contribution, which could be worth billions of dollars, would give the next generation of Americans a stake in the company's future.
"SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit."
SpaceX, whose shares were trading just above $127 Wednesday, said it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account.
SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell also announced a separate personal donation of more than 2 million shares of the company's stock.
Musk pledged last month to give every child in America a share of SpaceX in 2027, although he did not provide details at the time about how the proposed giveaway would work.
"Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk wrote on X in October.
SpaceX confirmed Wednesday that his latest commitment is part of that pledge.
‘DATA CENTERS IN SPACE’: FCC CLEARS SPACEX FOR 1M SATELLITES TO ‘EXTEND AMERICA’S LEAD IN SUPERINTELLIGENCE’

With the holiday season approaching, the pledged contributions represent another boost for the program, which provides tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children under 18 with valid Social Security numbers.
More than 3 million friends and family members have contributed to individual accounts, with total deposits exceeding $9 billion when philanthropic gifts and federal seed contributions are included, according to a Treasury Department statement provided to FOX Business.
Children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, are eligible for a one-time $1,000 seed contribution from the federal government.
While Trump Accounts have been created for eligible children under 18, parents and guardians must claim the accounts before they can manage them or enable contributions.
